news.title: Gavin Newsom Is Ready for His Next Act. Are Democrats Interested In Watching It?
news.text:
“Slick,” Newsom ventures when I ask what he assumes people say when his name comes up in 2028 speculation. With his dazzling white teeth, open collar, and hair Brylcreemed to a silver sheen, it’s not a bad guess. I had another association in mind: California itself.
“God, how lucky am I?” he replies, reflexively.
Answers may vary.
This summer I went to meet Newsom and found him in a sunbaked shopping plaza near downtown Las Vegas. He’d just wrapped up the last state budget of his eight-year term in office, leaving California with billions more in debt than when he arrived, and was visiting Nevada—a swing state, and the second, after South Carolina, on the Democratic primary calendar for 2028—to rally local Democrats and support a gubernatorial candidate named Aaron Ford. A handful of protesters stood in the parking lot, in 107-degree heat, flapping handmade posters that read “We Can’t A-‘Ford’ California.”
Newsom has been prepping for ever-higher office since he ran for mayor of San Francisco 23 years ago. But California remains the quintessential liberal hellscape of the national imagination and perhaps Newsom’s biggest impediment to any White House designs: nation-leading poverty and income inequality, and that pervasive and widespread homelessness you read about.
“I get all that,” Newsom counters. “Look, there’s a whole industry that’s been created to attack our state, and it’s pretty ironic. We’re the tentpole of the US economy. Think about where Donald Trump would be today if he didn’t have California. It’s the only thing holding up GDP growth.”
Newsom calls it “California derangement syndrome,” his spin on the MAGA attack line for Trump haters. He giddily machine-guns facts and quasi-facts about California and his governance thereof: the first major decline in people sleeping on the streets in nearly two decades, a 59 percent jump in housing construction (his housing number has since come under scrutiny for excluding major areas like San Diego), a $25 minimum wage for health care workers (federal minimum wage is $7.25). And did you know California is home to more Nobel laureates than anywhere else in the country?
When we met, Newsom was taking a victory lap after the passage of Proposition 50, which could flip five congressional seats in California in a tit-for-tat response to newly drawn seats in Texas meant to tilt the midterms in favor of the GOP. It was a controversial move, a sign of Newsom’s willingness to get down in the mud and beat Republicans at their own game. Democrats thrilled to it, giving Newsom a shiny trophy to campaign on.
While he spoke to Nevada canvassers, somebody yelled out “President!” and Newsom did a sheepish cut-the-mic gesture at his neck, signaling he wasn’t ready to go there. Oh, but he is. Submitting himself to a Vanity Fair interview, under fluorescent lights in an empty back room of a local ministry, he comes off as loose and playful, dodging and parrying like a political athlete, part salesman, part jocular bro, with just enough comic self-deprecation to make the whole soufflé rise. Earlier, when he was presented with a baseball jersey by local pols, Newsom pretended to unbutton and remove his shirt for a quick change, saying, “I’ve been working out,” inspiring squeals and wolf whistles.
But the more immediate and pressing question before Newsom—before he ever has a chance to try explaining California to middle America—is whether his charms can tame a restive and dyspeptic Democratic Party currently besotted with democratic socialists. The political progeny of Bernie Sanders are gaining ground from New York to Michigan on promises of burning the billionaire class to the ground, eager to cast the likes of Newsom as not only the avatar of California’s gross income inequality, but the model of a failed and corrupt establishment.
A clue to how Newsom might navigate the rocky terrain comes almost as soon as we sit down. I notice, as he starts talking, a vintage hand gesture: the thumb resting on bent forefinger to emphasize a point, unmistakably borrowed from a certain former president. “I watch videos of Clinton,” he tells me. “I seek his counsel, his advice, and even in his absence, do that. I’ve been a student of his from day one.”
The two have an actual relationship, talking late at night about strategy and ideas, including how to tackle the California problem. “He calls me late at night, wanting to talk about it, and he goes, ‘I’ve been thinking just nonstop about this. I just think you represent what they fear.’”
“He’s very mindful of that,” Newsom says. “It’s a problem to be solved, and no greater problem solver in that respect than Bill Clinton, in my mind. Master of his craft. Next-level.”
Invoking Clinton would seem a risky maneuver, not least because of Clinton’s apparent association with Jeffrey Epstein, but also because the man critics called “Slick Willie” is the very model of the kind of compromised liberalism the new left reviles. Clinton’s public favorability is middling at best, rating well below Sanders, the closest thing to a genuinely popular Democrat. (Clinton has denied having any knowledge of Epstein’s crimes and wrongdoing. He declined to be interviewed for this story.)
With a decision to run for president just over the midterms horizon—“I don’t think you have the luxury of much more time,” he tells me—Newsom is pitching himself as the Reasonable Man, a seasoned technician of center-left governance who steered the fourth-largest economy in the world with one hand and fought MAGA with the other. He is even drafting policy ideas and calling it Project 2029. After years of herding his state’s liberal cats, Newsom treats the new breed of progressive ideologues—New York mayor Zohran Mamdani being the exemplar—as Johnny-come-latelies.
“So much of what the DSA is promoting, I’m like, Been there, done that,” says Newsom, pointing to Assembly Bill 1482 as the “most progressive rent control in America.” “I’m the biggest climate champion that you know, but I’m not antibusiness.”
The Democratic Socialists of America trades in “slogans,” Newsom observes. When he sees Democrats applauding for what he calls “pablum and rhetoric,” he asks, “For that?”
Newsom may look like a chip off the Nancy Pelosi bloc (they’re distantly related and share a donor base), but that doesn’t mean he’s part of any so-called establishment. “Well, I’m not,” he insists. “I’m not. I mean, I’ve been at this awhile. To the extent I’m established, in that context—but I’m notoriously a disrupter at heart. I’ve never been for the status quo. Quite the contrary. I have a record that consistently challenges the status quo, and I tend to take risks to a degree that few elected officials do.”
Sounds like a sales pitch. Before we leave Vegas, Newsom invites me to California to see him in his natural habitat. “Bring security,” he jokes. “And bring extra money.”
“I’ve got my OSHA-approved hair,” he jokes to a small group of helmeted functionaries standing inside a half-built apartment complex in Chinatown. “I got a waiver a few years ago.”
Decked out in six feet three inches of blue suit, he’s signing a bill meant to speed up housing construction. California remains a brutal state for the working class and poor. I ask him why it took eight years to get to housing reform when he might have done it in his first hundred days. “I didn’t have the political capital,” he tells me flatly.
Newsom also credits Ezra Klein, the New York Times columnist, for pressuring him during a podcast conversation and in his 2025 book, Abundance, to dig into the environmental laws that block infrastructure and housing. “Ezra kicked my ass,” he says. “I respect my critics. I love them. Thank them. Pay attention to them.”
Newsom has been crowing about a 9 percent drop in unsheltered homelessness over the past year, though the numbers are in dispute. The state’s Legislative Analyst’s Office argues that they’re underreported. Newsom vetoed a bill meant to improve accountability, arguing that it was “duplicative.”
Klein, for his part, is reluctant to take credit for Newsom’s come-to-Jesus on housing, pointing to other intense political pressures. But he agrees with Newsom himself that Clinton is an accurate political ancestor.
“I think a lot about Bill Clinton when I think of Gavin Newsom,” Klein tells me. “The thing that defined Bill Clinton, his political strength, was to reconcile opposite political tendencies and, at the same time, to fluidly move with reality. You can say that of Gavin: He changes and adapts. I think that’s been his great political strength.” (Klein declined to weigh in on Newsom’s broader prospects.)
When the DSA championed a one-time 5 percent tax on California’s billionaires, they painted Newsom’s opposition as proof he was “trying to protect 250 prospective 2028 presidential donors, even if that means 3 million of his constituents are medically bankrupted,” as liberal journalist David Sirota put it. Newsom, openly worried about losing his tax base, parried with his own proposal, a national billionaire’s tax. Upon close inspection, it was more of a federal tax-bracket adjustment for people making over $100 million and headlined with a populist slogan. But it performed a neat piece of political jujitsu: blunting the attack from his left flank while inviting cries of “socialist!” from the right, thereby burnishing his progressive cred.
Even a master cynic like Steve Bannon, the MAGA philosopher king who was an early guest on Newsom’s podcast, This Is Gavin Newsom, can’t help but be impressed by his tactical chutzpah: “Game respects game.” Of Prop 50, Bannon told me: “He smoked us on that,” effusing about Newsom’s brinkmanship, predicting he’ll be a “hero” if the Democrats manage to take the Senate and adding, “Having Gavin Newsom as president wouldn’t be the worst thing in the world.”
But, Bannon hastens to add, he doesn’t think Newsom is built for what’s coming. “He doesn’t understand the moment he’s in,” Bannon says. “Every morning, he’s got to wake up and think about who he is that day. And what he stands for. That’s not the time we’re in. He’s trying to glide on the surface of a deep civil war within the Democratic Party.”
I remind Newsom that Bannon, in their podcast conversation, predicted he would become an “economic populist,” the ideology now animating the far left as it did Bannon’s nationalist right. “It’s a really interesting insight that’s staring me now in the face,” Newsom admits.
Last spring, Newsom had a private meeting with Senator Elizabeth Warren, who was in San Francisco supporting taxes on billionaires. Her advice to him: “Name the villain.” “I felt like I was getting schooled a little bit,” Newsom says of the meeting. “I don’t have a problem with the villain. This notion that if you’re successful somehow, you’re the villain, or you had a stroke of luck, you’re a villain, I have a harder time with.”
Newsom is, in that sense, a villain.
“I don’t begrudge other people’s success,” he continues, citing his own wine business, PlumpJack, which he launched in 1992, when he was 24. A recent estimate pegged his net worth at roughly $30 million, with an annual income of about $2 million, according to recent tax filings. He owns two houses, worth an estimated $16.5 million. “I just don’t feel that. I’d be faking that. That’s inauthentic of me to say that. I aspire to it. I think it’s actually one of the things that’s always frustrating about my party. I’m a small-business person, and I intimately appreciate the risk-taking and the contribution of businesses. And I don’t think you could be pro-job and antibusiness.” The devil, he says, “is in the details.”
“But,” he finishes, “I believe billionaires should pay more taxes. Period. Full stop. One hundred percent.”
The brightest red line for the rising DSA is calling Israel’s military campaign in Gaza a genocide. Last March, Newsom agreed that Israel was in effect an “apartheid state” but then walked it back, suggesting he was misunderstood. When I ask him about it, Newsom tells me the media was “wildly overreading my first comments” and “wildly overreading the second comments.”
He wasn’t calling Israel an apartheid state, he says, but he wasn’t not calling it one either. “You’re dealing with the one guy—the only guy?—who brought a field hospital to Gaza. No one else did. I also can’t stand antisemitism. It sickens me to my core.”
He mentions Jewish family members on his wife’s side and says words like Zionist and genocide are “loaded terms that mean many different things to many different people, and I could play into those binaries. People aren’t going to listen to a damn thing you say unless you’re willing to align with a word.”
He still refuses to call what happened in Gaza—more than 73,000 Palestinians killed by Israel since Hamas attacked and killed 1,200 and abducted 251 hostages on October 7, 2023—a genocide, even when I push him on it repeatedly. “I’m not able to objectively conclude that,” he tells me. “Were there war crimes? Crystal clear...but I’ll leave that to the courts in more objective lines because it relates to the pure definition.”
It’s a Newsomian reflex: Refuse the label, keep both audiences half satisfied, and let the ambiguity do the political work a position never will. “Nuance,” he says. “Nuance.”
Newsom takes a similarly tactical approach to artificial intelligence, probably the defining issue of the coming presidential cycle. Two years ago, California’s legislature voted for the first state bill regulating AI, Senate Bill 1047, sponsored by state senator Scott Wiener, who wanted to make AI companies liable for harm caused to society. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei wrote Newsom that the bill’s “benefits likely outweigh its costs,” while OpenAI and the Trump-aligned venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz opposed it, the latter launching a public campaign and hiring a Newsom confidant as a lobbyist. Newsom pal Ron Conway, the venture capitalist and Democratic mega-donor who has stakes in OpenAI, Anthropic, and Mistral, called the bill “very, very ill-conceived.”
Newsom says that after he vetoed it, “people quietly said thank you.” He encouraged a narrower and less censorious bill based on a white paper he commissioned from various AI experts, including Fei-Fei Li. He announced his intention to sign the resulting bill, SB 53, at a 2025 Clinton Global Initiative event with Clinton, telling reporters, “We worked with industry, but we didn’t submit to industry.”
Newsom says if he were president he’d build a federal response to AI dangers based on California’s model: “I would be leading an international movement focusing on the issue of truth, and safety, and trust.” Conway argues that Newsom’s friendly relationship with AI leaders are a feature, not a bug. Newsom knows Sam Altman personally, so he’s uniquely positioned to broker solutions.
“There’s a lot of bullshit in this space,” Newsom says. “As much as I admire and believe in a lot of what I’m hearing from a lot of these folks, I also am mindful of capitalism, and mindful of a lot of self-dealing, and very mindful of the innovation that is important to maintain in this space.”
He has promised to “democratize the economy” and redistribute tech wealth, floating a version of Sanders’s idea for a sovereign wealth fund with a 50 percent public stake in AI companies, though Newsom won’t put a percentage on it and points to the Trump Accounts, Trump’s government-backed investments for children, as his favored model. “It’s just the bane of my existence not calling them Newsom Accounts.” Artificial intelligence is “putting the dagger in the heart of the status quo,” he says. “And so something big, bold has to be written, and so you’ve got to renegotiate this contract.”
Newsom says negotiating state AI laws has soured him on some of the tech leaders, though he won’t name them. “I’ve lost relationships with these guys,” Newsom says. “I don’t recognize them. What the hell happened to these people? I have animus now that I never had. I think power corrupts—how they’ve been able to corrupt and manipulate the political system.”
“I don’t care if they voted for Trump,” he continues. “They were always libertarian. But it’s the nature of just too much abundance, too much wealth, too much isolation, too much indulgence, and too much power. Because the money buys you power.”
For a second, he sounds like Sanders. Maybe Bannon was right?
Young Man in a Hurry, Newsom’s 2026 memoir, was an attempt to make himself seem like a real boy and not just a political Pinocchio. Though he stretches to make the case that he earned his own way in life—he grew up the son of a single mother in working-class circumstances—Newsom was well-connected before he was out of diapers. His father, William “Bill” A. Newsom III, went to an elite San Francisco prep school with Gordon Getty and John Paul Getty Jr., sons of the billionaire oil magnate J. Paul Getty, and served as the Getty family fixer in the 1960s and ’70s.
When Gordon’s parents divorced, he briefly moved into the Newsom household as a teenager. After Newsom’s parents filed for divorce in 1971, Newsom was unofficially adopted by Gordon, repaying the favor the Newsoms had extended decades earlier. Gordon took young Gavin and his sister, Hilary, on family vacations, including to watch whales in Canada and view elephants in Kenya. Newsom revels in the gossip of his own access: In 1973, when John Paul Getty III was kidnapped by the Calabrian Mafia in Italy—they cut off his ear and mailed it to the press, demanding $17 million for his safe return—it was Newsom’s father, whom Newsom calls the “consigliere to the Getty family in times of turmoil” in his book, who negotiated and arranged the delivery of a reduced $2.2 million to the kidnappers. When Paul finally made his way back to California, he went toy shopping with Newsom and his sister.
In the early 1990s, Gordon Getty seeded Newsom’s Napa Valley wine start-up, PlumpJack, which Newsom launched with Gordon’s son Billy and named after an opera Gordon had composed. Later, Newsom fell out with Billy over a property dispute involving a house they jointly owned. In his memoir, Newsom called the breakup “one of the great holes of my life.”
Newsom was a Gen X child. A superfan of Sylvester Stallone’s first Rocky movie, he set up a makeshift boxing ring in his backyard and held neighborhood matches. He went through a phase as an amateur magician called the Great Gavini. He based his clothes and hairstyle on Remington Steele, the 1980s TV show starring Pierce Brosnan as a charming con man, a confession some found baffling. More baffling still: He appears to have kept the look for life.
He majored in political science at Santa Clara University, admitted on recommendations from a member of the school’s board of regents and former governor Jerry Brown, a friend of his father’s. He received a partial baseball scholarship but never played in a game. A former teammate described it as “kind of the standing joke that Newsom played on the team.”
Newsom, for all his political storytelling, is transparent about his lifelong dyslexia, which shaped his mind in unusual and crucial ways. When reading a book or speech, he has to underline every word to track and make sense of it. Because he doesn’t work well with a teleprompter, he memorizes speeches in advance, which has made him quick with data and able to debate with alacrity. An operative in Sacramento tells me, “He has a mind like a steel trap that remembers absolutely everything.”
“You’ve never seen me read a speech,” Newsom has said, “because I cannot read a speech. Maybe the wrong business to be in.”
Newsom’s first foray into politics was volunteering for Willie Brown’s 1995 San Francisco mayoral campaign, which led to an appointment on the Parking and Traffic Commission, which led to an unelected seat on the Board of Supervisors. By the time he ran for mayor in 2003, Newsom had the backing of Brown’s establishment.
His defining political act as mayor was to advocate for gay marriage in 2004, a maverick move at a time when Democrats were treading carefully to avoid a wedge issue in the presidential election.
But while he married gay couples in the face of cultural headwinds, his own dating life sometimes eclipsed the headlines. Local press published power rankings of his “side pieces.” Kimberly Guilfoyle had previously dated Billy Getty before they were introduced at a political fundraiser. At the time, Guilfoyle was an assistant DA in San Francisco prosecuting a high-profile dog-mauling case and making the rounds on cable news. Game respects game: Their three-year marriage was seared into the public imagination with a 2004 photo spread in Harper’s Bazaar of the two spooning in eveningwear on the floor of a house owned by Gordon and Ann Getty. The story was titled “The New Kennedys.” When Guilfoyle started working for Court TV in New York, Newsom would review tapes of her broadcasts, critiquing her facial expressions. After they separated in 2004, Newsom had an affair with Ruby Rippey, the wife of his own deputy chief of staff Alex Tourk, which became tabloid fodder. (Rippey wrote about the affair, and her struggle and recovery from alcoholism, for Vanity Fair.)
Newsom met his wife, the actor and documentary maker Jennifer Siebel Newsom, on a blind date in 2006. When the night ended, Newsom recounts in his book, Jennifer discovered that her car was locked in a parking garage. Newsom invited her to stay over “platonically” at his house. “The living room had no sofa and the windows had no blinds,” he writes in his memoir. “To keep out the sun, I had taped rolls of black plastic over them. She later confessed that her first glimpse of my abode brought to mind a question: ‘Did this guy take his interior design inspiration from American Psycho?’”
Later she was living in his apartment when an actual psychotic stalker tried breaking into the building with a roll of duct tape. Police found a cassette tape in the man’s car labeled “President Newsom.”
The couple married in 2008, and Siebel Newsom was quickly cast in the role of stabilizing force, an attractive, wealthy, and engaged political partner for an aspiring politician. She developed her own feminist profile, producing documentaries about women in media and parenting boys, and in 2022 became the star witness at Harvey Weinstein’s Los Angeles sexual assault trial, testifying—under the designation Jane Doe #4—that Weinstein had raped her in a Beverly Hills hotel room in 2005.
(Weinstein’s defense attorneys argued the encounter was consensual, portraying her as a “self-confident, ambitious Stanford business school graduate” who had stayed in friendly contact with Weinstein afterward. The jury eventually convicted Weinstein but deadlocked on the counts related to Siebel Newsom.)
When I ask Newsom whether Siebel Newsom would make a good first lady of the United States, he doesn’t hesitate. “Oh God, yeah,” he says. “Next-level. I mean, she’s got the values, the competency. She’s got, you know, a learnedness. She’s got a point of view.”
“He didn’t try and run away from it,” says Conway. “He faced it head-on, and fought it head-on, and got the result he should have gotten. We defeated it.”
Newsom says the fight “was an extraordinary gift in some ways” because it caused him to reflect on who he was. “And that’s been a great process. Are there certain patterns?”
Not that he doesn’t regret dining at The French Laundry.
“Of course. It was boneheaded. It was a costly stress test. What the hell was I thinking?”
The political near-death experience appeared to embolden him for his next incarnation: the online alpha Trump fighter. “TINY HANDS IS OUT HERE COPYING ME—BUT WITHOUT THE STAMINA (SAD),” he posted on X last summer. As a former deputy communications director for the governor, Alex Stack, summed up the new Newsom worldview: “Politics is all content now.”
It was Newsom’s eldest son, Hunter, who alerted him to the content that defined Trump’s 2024 victory among young male voters. “When he started talking to me about Andrew Tate, I got nervous,” Newsom tells me, referring to the kickboxer-influencer and alleged sex trafficker who has denied wrongdoing. “He said, ‘Andrew Tate’s innocent. Hey, Dad, he’s in Florida. He’s coming to California. You should be with him.’ Like...no? And how do you know about this guy? And then he’s talking to me about Charlie Kirk, and he’s talking about Jordan Peterson, and I’m like, What the hell is going on? And then I look at his [social media] search, and it’s just, like, basketball.”
Newsom started his podcast explicitly to connect with young men, presenting himself as a Democratic problem solver and his own kind of alterna-bro. To book Kirk, his inaugural guest, Newsom connected through Guilfoyle. (“Obviously, they have a shared past,” Kirk later said.) I ask Newsom what he learned from his forays into the manosphere. “It’s the boyosphere,” he says, describing a world of online nihilists living at home with no romantic or financial prospects. “It’s not the manosphere. That’s the biggest revelation, and I think it’s a profoundly significant distinction.”
A Democratic strategist complains to me that Newsom is overly obsessed with the mechanics of politics—the platforms, the algorithms, the cultivated influencers—but “glitches out” when asked his vision for the country. Ro Khanna, the progressive congressman from Silicon Valley and a potential 2028 contender himself, tells me Newsom is ambition in search of an animating belief. “He wants the rhetoric of boldness without actually the courage of pissing people off,” Khanna says, citing the billionaire tax dodge. “The politician that Gavin Newsom most resembles is Bill Clinton.” Khanna doesn’t mean it in a positive way, arguing that Clinton was a “center-right” politician.
Mike Madrid, a cofounder of the Lincoln Project who advised a rival campaign against Newsom in 2018, hears versions of the same question everywhere he goes: opportunist or visionary? Newsom let down working-class Californians, especially Latinos, he says, but he won’t deny his political gifts. “Anybody who’s counting Gavin Newsom out is making a very, very big mistake,” he tells me. “He’s a truly generational talent, one of the most talented Democrats in the country.”
“He’s not afraid of confrontation,” he continues. “He’s not afraid of the attacks that are going to come on him. He leans into that, he understands how to turn attention into a strength, even if it’s negative. As long as the media spotlight is focused on him, he’s in contention.”
If that sounds like a description of Trump, it’s no coincidence. Newsom is probably the most studied politician in America, absorbing styles and ideas—whether Clinton’s thumb gesture or Trump’s media strategy—and making them his own with a Cheshire grin.
Newsom can come off as hammy and performative onstage—his cadences sometimes call to mind William Shatner as Captain Kirk—but he insists that whatever conviction looks like, he has a battle-hardened version of it. “They want a fighter,” he says of Democrats. “And the good thing is, look, I can back up a lot of the rhetoric, and that’s the difference. I’ve been at this long enough. I’ve got receipts, and I know what works.”
But former vice president Kamala Harris is threatening to crowd the centrist Californian got-the-receipts lane in a prospective Democratic lineup and already polling higher than Newsom among likely 2028 voters. In interviews, Newsom has slimed her with the faintest praise, talking about her like she’s retired since her 2024 loss to Trump (“she’s lived an extraordinary life”) and suggesting in an interview with Axios that she might run for office again, such as “school board.”
In our interview, Newsom suggests she’s weak, complaining that the Harris campaign in 2024 didn’t stand up for California’s Medi-Cal expansion to undocumented immigrants, a policy he had shepherded into law, after it came under attack from Trump and JD Vance. “Everyone criticized me during the Harris campaign for that,” says Newsom. “We’re practicing it. Now you’re running away from it.”
In September, Newsom told CNN that he wouldn’t run for president in 2028 if Harris ran, though it may have been less a binding promise than a tactical signal to Black voters, especially in South Carolina, the first major primary state in the 2028 election, where he’d just visited. When I ask if he’d drop out of the race were Harris to announce her candidacy after him, he punts but adds: “You can’t hold off on making a decision, waiting, waiting, waiting. But I don’t think that will—I’m not concerned about that, candidly.”
I ask Newsom to imagine himself in a debate of primary candidates in 2028, facing off against the likes of New York congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, likely to scorch him for his political impurities. “Give me the time and I’m happy to give you the crime, as they say,” he says, reworking the original expression before catching himself and adding, “I just mean that in the context of ‘politics is politics.’ ”
“I look forward to that debate,” he tells me. “Oh you better believe it.”
Newsom alleges that a fraud case against his former chief of staff, Dana Williamson, morphed into an investigation of Newsom himself. The case predates Trump’s term, and the alleged crimes didn’t take place in Newsom’s office, but once Trump was elected, Newsom claims, the Department of Justice went on a fishing expedition to get something on him. “Trump took it to the next level to go after us, came up with nothing, so they were like, ‘Find something,’ ” he tells me. “That’s abuse of power. And that’s when I said, ‘Enough.’ ” (Attorney General Todd Blanche has publicly disputed Newsom’s account.)
None of it has implicated Newsom personally, but it did highlight some gamy dealings, like the $4.28 million his wife’s nonprofit, the California Partners Project, received from donors with business before the state. Newsom helped pipe $1.05 million from a Sonoma County tribe to his wife’s nonprofit in 2023, then appointed the tribe’s chairman to the UC Board of Regents less than three months after the final payment, a sequence investigators are reportedly examining.
The transactions are legal under California’s permissive behested-payment rules, but none of it looks particularly ethical. Earlier this year, Newsom was fined $31,500 for failing to report more than $5.5 million in behested payments on time. He says he “screwed up on the paperwork” while trying to raise money for victims of the LA wildfires.
It was during the fires that Newsom had a tense encounter with Trump, poking a finger in his chest and gripping his arm on a tarmac and riding with him in a limo to Malibu, which Newsom details in his memoir, suggesting Trump was obsessed with him (telling him his wife was “hot”) and also personally hurt when Newsom attacked him at his own inauguration afterward, calling Newsom up to make sure they were still “good.”
I ask Newsom whether the appearance of self-dealing in the FBI investigation, even if legal, undercuts his ability to effectively attack the man he calls “simply the most corrupt president in American history.”
“No, total bullshit,” he says. “This is why he’s doing it.”
Game respects game.
For Newsom, the fight itself is the point. Whatever Trump throws at him, Newsom reframes it as proof that he, personally, is the one MAGA fears most, less a governor under a cloud of suspicion than the Democratic Party’s designated boss, martyred and re-martyred in real time, on-brand and ready for the next fundraising email. To wit: Within hours of announcing the DOJ investigation, Newsom sent out a fundraising blast and raised a quarter-million dollars in two weeks, leveling up a $14.4 million war chest ready-made for 2028.
It’s as close as he comes to expressing genuine doubt. Newsom’s ostentatious embrace of Clinton would suggest he believes Trump has realigned American politics to the right like Ronald Reagan did in the 1980s, and that a successful move for Democrats is a tack to the middle. But few people seem to believe the middle exists anymore, and Newsom’s critics question whether he has an actual vision. The first time I ask him, he stumbles.
“I think I do,” he says. “I certainly have, as a governor, from a governing perspective—from a campaign perspective, it’s a little different. How do you paint that picture of a journey we can all go on together, where everyone feels included?”
The second time I ask, following an appearance at the InterContinental hotel in Los Angeles, he still resists: “The hesitation is only because I don’t want to make it a campaign slogan, and I don’t have a campaign slogan for you.”
Newsom was arranging a tour of Southern states later in the summer, specifically to get his face in front of South Carolinians. It’s a chance, he says, to connect with the electorate and figure out his own gut. “You’ve got to start to feel it,” Newsom says, beating his chest. “You know, it’s the Nietzsche: ‘If you don’t have a big enough why you can’t endure the how.’ ”
The presidential campaign process will be an MRI on everything Newsom has ever said and done, and “who the hell needs to go out there and get the MRI on words?” But of course words matter, as Newsom well knows.
“My why is to stand up for ideals and strike out against injustice,” he says. “It explains more things in more ways on some of the things I’ve done over the last 20 years, personally and professionally. Number two: We’re all better off. So this fundamental notion of the commonwealth is deeply ingrained in my consciousness.”
Just when it seems he’s making it all up on the fly, he mentions a nascent platform he’s been sketching out, which he dubbed Project 2029 after the MAGA blueprint Project 2025. “I’ve quite literally written out, like, eight pages of commonsense good policy ideas that are long overdue, that would be a framework of a 2029 plan,” he tells me.
Later, in the same conversation, the page count grows: “I have, I kid you not, 36 pages of ideas.” He has notebooks of ideas in his car, he says, and invites me to see them. So we get into an elevator and head down to the subbasement of the hotel, arriving at a delivery entrance pungent with garbage smells and a team of stone-faced Secret Service agents hovering around the governor’s black SUV. He opens the back door and rifles through a leather duffel bag, pulling out a pile of notepads and loose-leaf paper filled with handwritten scrawl. He flips through, reading off bits and pieces, until he gets to a page marked “PROJECT 2029: Ideas for Democrats.”
“No one touches these,” he says. “These are my own little version. This is just policy, not narrative, the kinds of things we need to do: zoning reform, corporate tax, junk-fee stuff, new domestic strategies and tariffs, preschool things, a cap on childcare, family leave, paid sick leave, child tax credits, industrial decarbonization, anti-monopoly stuff, immigration, whistleblower protections.”
I ask if this stuff is for January 6, 2029, the day a new president is certified by Congress. He smiles coyly. I note that Bobby Kennedy also toured the South in 1968 during his own run for the presidency. At this, Newsom brightens, mentioning a framed photograph at home, a black-and-white image of Kennedy kneeling in front of a young boy next to an old beat-up car. Newsom says he looks at the image while he brushes his teeth every morning. He gets down on one knee to imitate the Bobby Kennedy pose in the garage of the InterContinental.
“Yeah, that’s the why,” he muses. “Let’s stand up for ideals.”
Newsom loves the performance. The Rocky Balboa of it all, the Bill Clinton of it all, the Bobby Kennedy of it all.
He will undoubtedly draw punches from both ends of the political divide, both saying essentially the same thing: slick, shallow, failed, corrupt, cynical, visionless. And, of course, Californian. Can Newsom survive the debate this country wants to have?
“I don’t have a problem fighting,” Newsom tells me. “Nor do I have a problem getting roughed up and getting back up. I’ve been road tested. It’s not small ball out here in California.”
His chin is out and ready.
news.summary: As the governor looks beyond California, he opens up about his political ambitions, his vision for the country, and why he's chosen Bill Clinton as his 2028 spirit animal.

news.title: The gospel according to Andy Beshear
news.text:
Andy Beshear has a favorite song: “Universal Sound” by Tyler Childers, the Grammy-winning country artist with a special place in the Kentucky governor’s heart. That title is something of a metaphor, about connecting to a deep, abiding spirituality accessible to us all. It’s meant to be an ecumenical message — just like the one Beshear hopes to deliver.

“Universal Sound” carried him through a “nasty” reelection campaign in 2023, which ended with a comfortable victory over his GOP opponent, state Attorney General Daniel Cameron, who had been hand-picked for the race by Sen. Mitch McConnell. Amid mounting speculation that Beshear could become a leading contender in the 2028 Democratic presidential primary, “Universal Sound” may well become familiar to more voters.

Beshear’s newly published book, which is de rigueur for potential candidates seeking to raise their political profile and lay out a vision, is also stoking talk of 2028. With its title taken from the biblical parable of the Good Samaritan, “Go and Do Likewise: How We Heal a Broken Country” explores how President Donald Trump and his administration have, in Beshear’s words, “hijacked” Christianity, and how the governor’s brand of inclusive faith underpins his political life, offering readers a blueprint for governing with compassion. 

I interviewed Beshear last week on the sidelines of Bourbon & Beyond, the music festival held annually in Louisville, Kentucky. He spoke about a reinvigorated religious left, addressed the tricky question of whether Trump should be considered a Christian, discussed his willingness to take unpopular stands in a red state, hinted at his plans for 2028 and explained why, as a politician often compared to Mr. Rogers, his kindness shouldn’t be mistaken for weakness. (Full disclosure: My husband, the novelist Silas House, served as Kentucky poet laureate under Beshear, and I once briefly assisted the governor on a writing project.) 

This conversation, which took place in a backstage trailer vibrating from the country and hip-hop tunes emanating from nearby stages, has been edited for length and clarity.

Governor, thank you for taking the time to talk. “Go and Do Likewise” is centered around the parable of the Good Samaritan from the Bible. What do you think that story has to tell us and teach us today? 

Well, it’s a perfect story for a moment of division. So the parable of the Good Samaritan is about a man lying bloodied and naked on the side of the road, and everybody that looks like him and thinks like him and votes like him and prays like him and loves like him goes to the other side of the road, ignores him and walks on. But Jesus chooses someone who’s raised to hate that man on the side of the road — the man on the side of the road was raised to hate the Samaritan — and that’s the person he has come over, not kick the man while he’s down, but lift him up, carry him to safety and, if you read it carefully, pay for his healthcare moving forward.

But the parable of the Good Samaritan is more than just a story to emulate; it’s an instruction, because Jesus then looks at the crowd and says, “Now go and do likewise” . . . This is one of the fundamental — not teachings but instructions of the Bible. It’s for us to be good, especially when it’s hard. For us not to judge people, and at people’s worst moments, to just be good to each other.

Faith is obviously so important to you, and I’ve heard you many times refer to it as your “authentic why.” What do you mean by that?

Well, first, I would never impose my faith on anyone. I’m not somebody who thinks that my faith needs to be written directly into law. That’s Christian nationalism, and I’m against that. But I do think in an age of authenticity — when your Instagram video is important and your TikTok video is important — people want to know you, what drives you. They don’t have to agree with what drives you. They just want to see that it drives you to do good. And for me, that is my faith. 

It tells me I’m supposed to leave this world a little better than I found it, and that’s one of the reasons I’m still [here]. You know, I thought that two terms as governor would be enough, and they still may be. But I see a world now that’s moving backward and not forward. And doesn’t faith call you to stand up and to speak out at that moment?

What do you think being in that position — I imagine you sitting there in Frankfort at night, weighing this [calculus] — has taught you?

First, I believe in any job that I’ve taken on. I am fully dedicated to the people of Kentucky, and when I fight with the president, it’s not because I’m a Democratic governor and he’s a Republican president. It’s because he’s doing something that hurts the people of Kentucky, and whether it’s popular or not, that was the job I took on to do my very best to move us not right, not left, but forward.

But you know, [the COVID pandemic] taught me a lot of lessons. I did what I thought was the right thing, that might not be the popular thing, the thing that would save the most lives. And you know what I found? As long as you’re willing to respect people enough to explain your why and not just your what, doing the right thing is oftentimes the politically popular thing, even if it wasn’t beforehand. People respect conviction, even if they don’t necessarily agree with it. And when you’re willing to explain why you did something, people can disagree with you but still believe you’re coming from a good place.

One thing I’ve been thinking about as I read your book is that the religious left used to be such a strong force in American politics. You know, Bobby Kennedy, all of his work —

All of the War on Poverty, even if not couched in those terms —

Yes. Bobby Kennedy’s work for social justice was rooted in his Catholicism. Jimmy Carter, famously a Sunday school teacher, spoke about his faith a lot. Even Hillary Clinton, in her husband’s 1992 presidential campaign and administration, talked about her faith and took a lot of flak from establishment media. What happened to the religious left? Why do you think it declined, or kind of went underground?

Well, what I think we’re seeing now, when you see the James Talaricos of the world, our Kansas Senate candidate [Democrat Adam Hamilton] who’s a Methodist minister and others . . . you know, the media will always try to take something as a tactic. They’re like, “Why are Democrats talking more about faith right now?” instead of “Why are people of faith running as Democrats right now?” And I think it’s because there is such a manipulation and a hijacking of faith going on, in such a transparent manner, that people of faith are saying, “I’ve had enough.”

When you see Donald Trump hold a Bible in a way that you’re pretty sure he’s never held it, much less never read it; when he says he doesn’t think there’s any way he’s going to heaven, he doesn’t seem to be worried about it; when he walks out after Erika Kirk gives voice to the Golden Rule in such a beautiful way, and says, No, no, I believe in the exact opposite; when you see JD Vance using faith to kick people while they’re down instead of lift them up, and to judge as many people as possible — then I think people of real faith want to stand up and take that back. Or at least to provide the counterexample. I think people are tired of seeing faith used for bad in public life instead of for good, and that’s the core of why I wrote the book.

You don’t shy away from going after President Trump. You write that he “makes people feel good about themselves by telling them it’s okay to be the worst version of themselves.” At another point you say, “Trump may occasionally talk about Jesus (or ‘Two Corinthians’), but he has missed the point. Jesus lifted up the very people this Republican administration pushes down . . . Trump throws Gatsby parties with his billionaire friends, while Jesus hung out with the exact opposite. Trump clears the very people out of city parks that Jesus would minister to.” 

That’s a powerful indictment. You’re saying that the president doesn’t love his neighbor as himself.

No, he calls his neighbor “the enemy from within.” It is the most stark contrast. I think about “love your neighbor as yourself” versus the president [characterizing] your neighbor as the enemy from within. I also think about Erika Kirk saying, I forgive my enemies, and Donald Trump saying, no, I hate my enemies . . . It’s just the exact opposite of what the Bible is supposed to teach us.

At one point, you question if he even knows the story of the Good Samaritan. 

I’m not sure he does.

Christ said, “You will know them by their fruits,” right? Do you think President Trump is a Christian?

I try not to question people’s faith, because I admit that that is judging. But he is not living and he is not governing like a Christian. Now, when you think about the miracle of the fishes and the loaves in each of the four first books of the New Testament, it’s that important. Jesus, in a time of scarcity, makes sure everybody has enough. Donald Trump has repeatedly tried to take food off kids and seniors’ table [and] was willing to use starving Americans as leverage during a government shutdown. That is not living or governing like a Christian, and I doubt they ever run out of food at the White House. 

I think about the “Big Ugly Bill,” and it’s causing kids to lose having enough food, but it’s also taking doctors away from the sick. And while I think he was talking about spirituality, the actual words of the Bible — which many people believe is the direct word of God — is that Jesus said a doctor is for the sick. Yet there’s a lot of sick [people] that aren’t going to have a doctor. So Donald Trump certainly isn’t living out faith. And for those that preach that he is a person of faith, my granddad, a lay Baptist minister, always said, you know, faith without action —

Yeah, is “dead.” In the book you call for a “Great American Reset.” What do you mean by that? How would you define that?

I did not live through McCarthyism, but we have read about McCarthyism — about attacking and othering people, throwing them in jail — and Donald Trump’s doing it right now. He’s so desperate, he’s calling people communists. I mean, just blatantly ripping off Joseph McCarthy. But the president himself is doing it. But we reached a point where people said enough, and they took a breath, and we came back together and did not repeat it — at least until now. 

I don’t want to leave a broken country to my kids or to anyone else’s. I don’t want to leave this divided of a country to anyone else. I don’t want to leave a country where we are told it’s OK to hate each other and that your neighbor is the enemy. And so while I judge MAGA politicians, I don’t judge MAGA voters — and I don’t even use that phrase. Why? Because I want them to take a breath and to say, “OK, you know, let’s do something better. You know, this went too far. Let’s repair the wounds that we have,” so that we don’t move from retribution from one side to retribution to another side, and back and forth and back and forth, but that we get something more like what we had growing up. 

When you were talking, I thought of another scripture — “the repairer of the breach” from the Book of Isaiah, which Bill Clinton used quite a bit. That’s kind of what you’re talking about, bringing people back together, healing divides.

I feel like we’ve done that better in Kentucky than most places. I still don’t always agree with the way people vote, but if you look at where we were with [my predecessor as governor] Matt Bevin, [who was] going after everybody who is different, othering anyone and everyone, judging everyone . . . Look at where we are now. That last [presidential] election, you didn’t see nearly the signs or the flags or anything else. You saw people who, in the very least, wanted to genuinely respect their neighbors.

You talk about that happening here in Kentucky. How do you think that can begin nationally, though, when a lot of MAGA Republicans out there think, as you write in the book, that “Democrats are Satan in the flesh”?

Well, Republicans right now are costing them about $4,500 extra a year in tariffs, about $800 extra a year in gas. If they need diesel, it’s even worse. So they might think that Democrats are Satan in the flesh, but Republicans are bankrupting them. If you want to eat, to be able to afford groceries for yourself or your kid, if you want to be able to see a pediatrician for your child in your own community, you’re going to think about things a little bit different. Democrats have the chance to grab that lane. And we should be. That’s where we should want to be. That’s certainly where I’ve always governed. 

Think about a soybean farmer, and you and I both know we got a lot in Kentucky, and I’m not sure if any of them voted for Kamala Harris. But look at what’s happened to them. First, the USAID program’s eliminated. That’s one of their major clients, because if you feed starving nations, people like the United States better. Then [Education Secretary] Linda McMahon comes in, using her wrestling knowledge, to end the farm-to-cafeteria program. Then Donald Trump — and he alone decides on tariffs — throws them on China, and they stop buying our soybeans. They’re the largest purchaser in the world. They move to Brazil and Argentina.

Then he decides to get in a war with Iran that he doesn’t even explain to the American people a couple days before in his State of the Union. And now the price of diesel, which runs all farm equipment, is at an all-time high. If that’s not enough, a third of the world’s fertilizer runs through the Strait of Hormuz. So, a soybean farmer that voted for Donald Trump, who believed that was their guy, is totally betrayed, trying to decide if they’re going to plant crops at all, or if Donald Trump has bankrupted their family farm.

You’re the most popular Democratic governor in the country, according to the polls, and this book is introducing you and your beliefs to a whole other set of people, of potential voters. What are your plans for 2028?

Well, I haven’t made any final decisions, but I will say when I walked off the stage in 2023 . . . I looked at [my wife] Britainy, and I said, “Hoo, I’ll never have to run for anything ever again.” As I’m here today, I’m not sure that’s the case anymore. And I’ll make that decision later. 

But I think about two core tenets of my faith. Number one, that I am made by a loving God that calls me to love other people, and that ought to be the baseline. And number two, I ought to leave things better than I found them. 

Listen: When you’re governor of a place you love, it’s enough. It’s special. What we’ve done in Kentucky together, all of us, people of all different parties over the last seven years, [has] been transformational, and I couldn’t be more proud — and I was willing to go out on top . . . But I can’t watch a country slide back. I can’t see progress that folks in Selma marched for 60 years ago, undone by a rogue Supreme Court. So I don’t know exactly what my role will be in the future, but I just will not leave a broken country to my kids or anyone else’s. I will not.

I want to ask you sort of a different question. Let’s say that a popular Democratic governor, who has been elected twice to that job in what many see as one of the reddest states in the country, decides to run for president. What would they offer the American people?

Well, a vision of both reviving the American dream, of proving to people [who] believe the economy is broken that it can work again. That if you work hard and play by the rules that you can get ahead — that you can take your kids on the same vacation that you went on, that you can leave your family better off. That we can fix the darn government that people look at as corrupt right now, and we can heal this divide that is such a threat to our future as Americans. And none of us enjoy — none of us wants to be mad at the person that lives across from us. I think we can get back to being, yes, an imperfect nation, but one that’s stable, [where] at least we are moving toward progress each and every day.

Right now, polls are showing that Democratic voters want fighters, leaders who are unafraid of punching back against corrupt and MAGA politicians. Some Democratic politicians are resorting to using strong language, dropping F-bombs to get their point across. You, by contrast, have built your political identity on leading with kindness. “Kentucky’s Mister Rogers” is how many people see you. One of your book’s chapters is titled “Be the Adult in the Room.” So I wonder if you think there’s room for that kind of politics in the party and America today, coming in the wake of Donald Trump.

Don’t mistake kindness for weakness. If I’m Kentucky’s “Mister Rogers” — he went up against Trump before Trump. He went up against a Republican incumbent governor that attacked him every day for four years, and the “Mister Rogers” is the one still standing. A lot of people can claim they’re fighting in different ways from the bluest of states. How many people have sued [Trump] 30-plus times from the reddest of states? How many people speak out against him when it could negatively impact their approval rating instead of positively impact their approval rating? 

You know, every day that I stand up for Kentuckians and Americans, every day that I fight back against this administration, I have more to lose than anybody else. But what’s an approval rating worth if you’re not going to use it for something? So there are different ways to fight, and here’s what I’d say to a lot of people: If somebody’s yelling, and you yell back, then nobody can hear a thing. There’s effective ways to defeat that person to fight and win. But shouldn’t we want one that will actually win in the end? And so I think that when people look at who’s fighting in the hardest of places, they see this governor. 

The midterms are about six weeks away. What do you think the Democratic Party is getting right, and where do you think it’s falling short?

I think that they are getting right how hard the world is on American families right now. I hate to use the “affordability” word, because I believe it’s becoming like a political science term. What it really [means] is that your medical bills cost too much. That’s why we forgave $250 million in medical debt here in Kentucky [via executive order]. It’s that your utility bill is going up. It’s that groceries are too much, and my goodness, gas is through the roof. We need to make sure that we’re communicating in terms that the American people communicate in. 

You said something at a recent book event that caught my ear, that the Democrats have gone too far on a few things. I’m wondering what those might be.

We went too far on overregulation. We’ve got to protect our environment, we’ve got to protect our workers. But if we make things so onerous, then it takes a long time to accomplish anything. If you believe we need more housing, and it takes that much longer to build housing, then people lose out. If it takes too long to build a factory, you don’t have those jobs that pay the good wages. So we’ve got to have a sense of urgency . . . Democrats have to design our policies in a way to get results, and if we believe truly in something, even if we’re only 80% right on what the policy looks like, understanding if we get it done faster, it benefits more people.

You come from what many observers would call the party’s more traditional wing. Right now, there’s a lot of energy behind progressives like Dr. Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, and democratic socialists like Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Zohran Mamdani. Do you think there’s room in the party for this wide range of political identities?

I think — and you’re not doing it — but I think that the media tries to put everybody in a box to have a narrative. How many people in a Trump plus-30 state that have vetoed every anti-LGBTQ+ bill that [has reached] their desk would suddenly be lumped in as a moderate? And that’s not to suggest I view myself as a progressive. I just — I don’t view myself as either. I view myself as pragmatic.

Start your day with essential news from Salon. Sign up for our free morning newsletter, Crash Course.

My job is to stand up for my people and all their rights, live out my faith and to see everyone as a child of God, but [also] to solve problems. And that’s where Democratic governors are. You know, I think that this debate can play out in the House and in the U.S. Senate, where they might have different caucuses. But governors aren’t one of 50 or one of 24 in a party. You’re one of one, and your job, if you’re doing it right, is to get things done, to actually improve people’s lives. So, I can’t be as ideological as someone who votes on the amendment to the rule, right? My job has to be to figure out how to get the best results for our people on each and every day. 

Are you worried that Republican attempts to deploy terms like “communist” across the board will hurt the Democratic brand overall?

Oh, I think what the president’s doing is so hyperbolic and so transparent that people see right through it. There is only one elected official in the entire country actively engaged in socialism, and his name is Donald J. Trump. 

The definition of socialism is government ownership of the means of production, and he is the only person negotiating a U.S. government interest in a private company. But, you know, what you do is you call people the name that you’re worrying that you are, and so he’s calling people “communist.” So now that he’s engaged in socialism, which he is, what is the difference between that and communism? It is the people in charge enriching themselves, which he and his family are doing. It’s turning the police and the justice system into your own personal force, which is what he’s doing. You see in each and every one of these that the things that Trump is calling people is what he’s actively engaged in.
news.summary: Kentucky's governor on his new book, the Good Samaritan and why he hasn't ruled out 2028

news.title: One demographic is ‘ripping the heart out of Trump’s presidency,’ pollster warns
news.text:
President Donald Trump is being deserted by white non-college-educated voters ahead of the midterms, a phenomenon that is “ripping the heart out” of his presidency, according to CNN’s data analyst Harry Enten.

Speaking to John Berman on CNN News Central Tuesday, Enten was asked why the president had promised a new $15 billion steel plant in Iowa Monday.

“The target group of voters is white, non-college voters,” he answered. “They were the heartbeat of President Trump’s three presidential campaigns. And right now, the heartland is ripping the heart out of Donald Trump’s presidency.”

Enten pointed out that, two years ago, he was 25 points up on presidential rival Kamala Harris but is now on just -2.

“He’s now in the negative with white non-college voters!” he said. “He’s in the negative territory with a group of voters that fueled his three presidential bids and allowed him to win a second term in the White House back in 2024.

“We’re talking a drop here with the key core group of Donald Trump’s presidential campaigns, of 27 points away from the president of the United States. No wonder he’s so low.”

Asked how the situation compared with other presidents, Enten said that Trump is “more reliant on white non-college voters than any previous Republican president, and now he’s at the lowest of any Republican president, at this point in his second term among white non-college voters.”

He said that neither George W Bush nor Ronald Reagan nor Dwight D Eisenhower was as dependent on the group as Trump “and now even they have turned on him.”

Enten added that Bush had lost the House of Representatives and the Senate in his second-term midterms “in large part because a lot of voters who had previously been voting Republican decided to vote Democratic.”

The analyst concluded that the economy was the reason for the demographic’s disaffection with Trump, suggesting they had “decided to give [him] a second chance” because they had lost faith in Joe Biden’s stewardship of the economy – and now appear to feel his successor has proven no better.

“Oh my goodness gracious!” Enten said as he flashed up a graphic showing Trump’s approval rating on inflation with the group sliding from 24 points to -39.

“That’s a change of 63 points in the wrong direction, on the key issue that got Donald Trump re-elected to a second term, among the key group that got him re-elected,” he said.

Enten’s broadcasts have often made for uncomfortable viewing for the president in recent months, with the analyst last week presenting a 50 percent job disapproval rating for him and commenting: “They don’t just dislike him. There’s record hatred for the president of the United States going into a midterm.”

However, Trump himself posted a clip of Enten on Truth Social Tuesday in which he could be seen marveling at how solid his support is with MAGA die-hards, with whom he retains a 98 percent approval rating, down just one percent in two years, their faith seemingly unshakeable.

The same excerpt was also played by Jesse Watters on Fox News in a segment headed: “No cracks in the MAGA wall.” 

The White House has similarly pointed The Independent towards a recent Economist/YouGov poll highlighting his ongoing popularity among his base, which found 91 percent approval among MAGA voters, 79 percent among Republicans generally and 75 percent among people who voted for him in 2024. 

White House spokesperson Davis Ingle told The Independent: “No one can dispute the fact that President Trump has created one of the most robust coalitions in political history with the MAGA movement, and the president understands how to communicate with them.”

He characterized November’s vote as a clear choice between “doubling down on President Trump’s winning, commonsense agenda or the Democrats’ extreme liberal policies and obstruction.”
news.summary: A group that helped propel Trump’s return to the White House in 2024 are leaving him in droves, according to CNN

news.title: Trump tried to make burgers cheaper. It backfired spectacularly.
news.text:
On most fronts, President Donald Trump has shown little concern for reducing Americans’ cost of living ahead of November’s midterms. 
Trump has refused to accept Iran’s ceasefire proposals, even as the conflict pushes fuel costs to new heights. And he’s declined to abandon his trade wars — with US adversaries and allies alike — even as tariffs nudge up Americans’ expenses. 
Yet there is one area where Trump has recently tried to lower consumer prices in an economically coherent way, and it’s been a political disaster.

Key takeaways
• Trump relaxed tariffs on foreign beef, in hopes of lowering meat prices. • But the policy is too narrow to make much difference for consumers, shaving just a couple cents off the price of ground beef, in the best-case scenario. • Meanwhile, it antagonized cattle ranchers already hurting as a result of Trump’s trade conflicts and war with Iran. • The controversy appears to be dragging down Republicans in farm states.

In late August, the president lowered tariffs on up to 661 million pounds of imported lean beef trimmings, a key ingredient in hamburger meat.
This policy directly addressed a genuine problem facing US consumers: Ground beef prices were roughly 8 percent higher last month than they had been one year earlier. And unlike many of the White House’s other ideas for increasing affordability, the meat imports proposal comported with conventional economic logic: If you reduce input costs for meat processors, they’ll be able to sell beef at lower prices. 
By endorsing this reasoning, the Trump administration was implicitly rebuking its own theory of trade economics (which holds that tariffs increase costs for foreign companies, not American consumers). In doing so, Trump also put voters’ material interests — and economists’ conventional wisdom — above his ideological hangups.
And he’s paying dearly for it. 
Instead of appeasing cash-strapped shoppers, the beef imports policy has mostly just aggravated (already aggrieved) agricultural firms. All across the farm belt, cattle ranchers are incensed by Trump aiding their foreign competition — after the president had already depressed their sales through tariffs and increased their costs via his Iran war and immigration policies. 
Cowpokes aren’t alone in resenting the White House’s affronts to agricultural interests. In dark red states like Kansas and Iowa, Democratic candidates have become highly competitive, while Republicans are racing to distance themselves from the president, in part by going after his beef plan directly.
Which raises the question: How and why did Trump’s plan for cheaper hamburgers go so wrong?
The answer partly concerns that measure’s particular flaws. But it also reflects broader problems with the administration’s governance, which now threaten to cost Republicans badly: A persistent failure to account for its policies’ economic consequences, a reliance on symbolic, last-minute fixes instead of far-sighted planning, and inattention to the material concerns of voters — even those as deeply conservative as cattle ranchers.
Trump’s cheap beef policy is small potatoes
As a political matter, the fundamental flaw with Trump’s beef import policy is simple: Its benefits to individual consumers are minuscule while its costs to certain cattle ranchers are substantial.
Trump’s tariff exemption has a tiny impact on consumer prices for two reasons. First, it just doesn’t affect that much meat. Although 661 million pounds may sound like a lot, that adds up to only about 6.8 percent of America’s annual ground beef supply. And most of these imports go to restaurants and fast-food joints, since grocers tend to prefer fresh, domestic ground beef. 
Second, only a small fraction of beef importers’ savings is likely to pass through to consumers. When a meat processor sees the costs of imported beef fall, it will generally try to pocket as much of its savings as it can, perhaps passing a small chunk along to the distributors it contracts with.
The distributors will then try to retain as much of that small chunk as they can before passing a slimmer fraction of the initial savings along to retailers or restaurants, who will then try to do much the same before selling to customers. In this way, past USDA research has suggested that only about 19 percent of any decline in wholesale beef prices reaches consumers.
Combine this reality with the narrow scale of Trump’s tariff relief, and the consumer benefit becomes microscopic. According to the Purdue University economists Ken Foster and Bernhard Dalheimer, Trump’s policy will reduce wholesale ground beef prices by at most 1.41 percent. If only 19 percent of that decline passes through to consumers, as the USDA’s research suggests, then shoppers will pay just 0.27 percent less for ground beef. In other words, in the best-case scenario, Trump’s policy would knock about two cents off the price of a pound of hamburger meat. 
For context, that price has risen by $1.32 cents — or 23 percent — since Trump took office.
[Media: https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/qX9Td/4/]
Why cattle country is beefing with the White House
Looking at these numbers, one might ask: So what are these ranchers complaining about? If Trump’s policy only lets in enough cheap foreign beef to cut prices by a couple cents, how much could it really hurt domestic cattle producers?
It is true that the president’s tariff relief has not condemned cattle ranchers to penury. But it does hurt farmers more than it helps individual consumers for two reasons.
First, the impact is highly concentrated on certain cattle operations. The new imports soften demand for domestic cull cows — breeding females who’ve gotten old enough to be worth more dead than alive — because their meat tends to be low-fat. No ranch specializes in producing such cattle. But ranchers who happen to have older herds at the moment are more reliant on cull cow sales. 
Second, from the perspective of all ranchers, Trump’s policy sets a disconcerting precedent. To build a herd, ranchers must hold back young female cows today — passing up immediate earnings from selling their meat — so as to breed more future cattle, which won’t come to market for years. 
In effect, this means that ranchers must perennially sink money into bets on the trajectory of future beef prices. If there happens to be a hamburger glut when today’s calves become ripe for slaughter, then their investments could produce a shabby return. But this downside risk is typically offset by the potential for outsize gains: If beef prices soar three years from now, ranchers who rebuild their herds today will reap large profits.
Yet Trump policy threatens this upside: If the government makes a habit of letting in cheap foreign beef every time hamburger prices spike, then it will effectively lower the ceiling on domestic ranchers’ future profits. 
As Iowa Sen. Chuck Grassley, Kansas Sen. Jerry Moran, and dozens of other farm-state members of Congress put the point in a letter to Trump, “Cattle markets are cyclical, and ranchers use the upswings to prepare for the inevitable downturn.” The lawmakers therefore urge Trump to abandon any “intervention in the natural system” that might depress those upswings, so as not to “undermine the long-term viability of family-owned cattle operations throughout the supply chain.”
Trump’s unintentional war on agriculture
For these reasons, Trump’s beef tariff exemption was inevitably going to attract more complaints from ranchers than applause for consumers. What’s made it especially politically toxic, however, is the broader policy context it emerged from. 
Simply put, when your foreign policy costs the average US household more than $500 in excess gasoline expenses — while your tariffs cost them $1,100 in elevated consumer prices — they’re probably not going to thank you for making a pound of ground beef two cents cheaper.
Meanwhile, ranchers may have been a bit less apoplectic about heightened foreign competition if Trump hadn’t already been squeezing them with his broader agenda.
Thanks largely to the president’s trade war with China, American beef exports fell 12 percent in 2025, as Beijing erected retaliatory barriers to US meat. This year, Trump’s trade war with Canada has further cut American farmers’ sales.
And while their foreign markets have been shrinking, US agricultural firms’ expenses have been skyrocketing due to the Iran War.
Farmers in general — and ranchers in particular — rely heavily on diesel fuel to power tractors, trucks, trailers, and myriad other agricultural machines. Thus, as the Iran War has throttled the global energy supply and triggered a record-breaking surge in diesel prices, US farmers have been hammered. 
In July 2026, American farms were paying 22 percent more for fuel than when Trump took office. Over the same period, fertilizer costs have risen by 8 percent, due to the Iran War’s impact on natural gas prices. 
[Media: https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/HSJwH/3/]
If this weren’t enough cause for farmbelt consternation, Trump’s immigration enforcement surge has provided an additional source of pain. Ranchers, like other farmers, rely heavily on the labor of immigrants, some of whom are undocumented. For this reason, US agricultural businesses have been wary of Trump’s approach to interior enforcement, despite their deeply conservative bent. 
Bizarrely, even as the administration has tried to placate rancher anger in recent weeks, it also launched a series of ICE raids targeted at beef-producing areas. These actions have triggered “work force disruptions” at feed yards and dairies — as immigrant workers were intimidated into staying home — according to a joint statement from the Cattlemen Associations for Texas, Oklahoma, and Kansas. The groups allege that thousands of cattle shipments have been delayed as a result, saddling producers with millions in lost revenue and unexpected costs.
Ironically, by engineering these ICE-induced disruptions, the White House also plausibly raised beef prices for consumers, undermining its own politically costly push for hamburger affordability.
Republicans are losing ground in the countryside
The political fallout from Trump’s beef policies — and broader affronts to agricultural interests — has been profound. 
Trump won Kansas in 2024 by more than 16 points. Yet Democratic minister Adam Hamilton is polling just 1.5 points behind sitting Republican Sen. Roger Marshall, according to a RealClearPolitics polling average. 
By itself, this could be chalked up to some peculiar, race-specific factor. But in Iowa, a farm belt state that went for Trump by 13 points in 2024, Democrats are also mounting improbably competitive campaigns. Democratic state representative Josh Turek leads Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson (who is publicly concerned about the beef issue) by half a point in polls of Iowa’s Senate race, while Democratic state lawmaker Lindsay James narrowly leads the House race in Iowa’s Second District, which Trump won by 10 points in 2024.
Meanwhile, in heavily agricultural Nebraska — where Trump beat Kamala Harris by more than 20 points — Democrat-aligned independent Senate candidate Dan Osborn is attacking Trump’s beef imports policy and running neck-and-neck with incumbent Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts. And in the Cornhusker State’s First District, which backed Trump by 13 points two years ago, Democrat Chris Backenmeyer is polling about two points behind the Republican incumbent Mike Flood.
Critically, Democrats’ gains in these jurisdictions don’t merely reflect the nationwide backlash against Trump and his party. The Democratic Party margin over Republicans in the national generic ballot is now about 9 points — a 10.5-point improvement over Harris’s showing in 2024. In the Iowa, Kansas, and Nebraska Senate races, Democrats are outperforming Harris’s showing by 13 points or more. 
Now, it’s conceivable that Democrats’ apparent strength in the farm belt could reflect some kind of systematic polling error. For example, if pollsters were undersampling less-educated rural white voters, then that might inflate Democratic candidates’ numbers more in agricultural states than in the country as a whole. 
But Republicans in the farm belt seem to think the rural backlash is real — and driven, at least partly, by Trump’s unintentional assaults on the agricultural sector.
A little bit of free trade goes a short way
Ultimately, the lesson of Trump’s ground beef fiasco isn’t that the president should have just ignored voters’ demands for cheaper meat — or economists’ warnings about tariffs’ negative impacts on affordability.
Had Trump prioritized low prices — and heeded basic economics — from day one, ranchers might still have ended up bitter about facing heightened foreign competition. But in a world without Trump’s trade conflicts or Iran War, such cattle producers would enjoy lower costs and larger foreign markets — and might therefore be more willing to take higher beef imports in stride. 
Meanwhile, if the prices of fuel and consumer goods were broadly lower, shoppers might be more appreciative of Trump’s economic governance. To be sure, even in that scenario, Americans probably wouldn’t notice the impact of loosening constraints on foreign lean beef trimmings. But if the administration were replicating such affordability measures across all policy fronts, the consequent savings could eventually add up to something large enough to attract voters’ notice and approval. 
In our world, however, Trump’s half-hearted embrace of ground-beef globalism was too little, too late. And in November, his party’s farm-belt candidates might pay the price.
