news.title: Will or won't they? Newsom and Harris weigh 2028 contest — and possible collision
news.text: The fraught relationship between Gavin Newsom and Kamala Harris is the stuff of reality TV. With their Hollywood looks and unbridled ambition, the two San Francisco-spawned Democrats have spent decades in tacit competition, ascending to the heights of California politics while still managing to avoid direct confrontation. That could change in 2028, should Newsom and Harris jump their parallel tracks and face each other — and possibly dozens of other candidates — in a bid for their party’s presidential nomination. California’s departing governor, who has spent the better part of his second and final term auditioning for the White House, recently said he wouldn’t run if Harris chooses to do so. “Mutual assured destruction,” Newsom called a he-she contest between the two Left Coast rivals, and a “waste of everyone’s time.” Some took that disavowal not as deference but jujitsu, or a form of political psy-ops directed at the governor’s longtime frenemy. In the same interview with CNN’s Jake Tapper, Newsom allowed as how the case against Harris — she’s a two-time loser at the presidential level and has had her shot — is “a pretty good one, actually.” “That’s objectively true,” Newsom added, driving the knife a little deeper. But rather than forcing Harris’ hand, Newsom’s professed willingness to stand aside may have simply invited the former vice president to take her sweet time deciding whether or not to run, waiting until the Democratic contest is well underway. And leaving Newsom in an odd sort of limbo. The former vice president, lips largely sealed, has done and said just enough to keep the door open to a 2028 run, without firmly committing to the contest. There’s a good chance that Harris — always careful, ever deliberate — doesn’t know what she'll do. Or, at least, isn’t 100% certain. She can afford to wait. After four years in the White House and her abbreviated 2024 White House bid, Harris has universal name recognition, a nationwide fundraising base and continued support among a significant number of Black women, who just happen to form the backbone of the Democratic Party. Harris won't freeze the presidential campaign the way she did the race for California governor. That contest was stalled and the field incomplete until Harris announced, after months of consideration, she'd take a pass. That's not to say, by any stretch, Harris is the favorite to win the presidential nomination. The criticism Newsom expressed — just a fella jawing away, as he and Tapper cast their fly rods — is a view that is widely held among Democrats. But the 2028 contest, which unofficially starts the instant the final polls close Nov. 3 — won't be firmly fixed until it's clear whether Harris is in or out. Newsom doesn't have that luxury of biding time, especially when so many other Democrats are poised to enter the race. The governor has his own formidable national fundraising base — thanks in good part to his online trolling and anti-Trump hijinks — and a not-small degree of name recognition across the country. But Newsom has yet to fully engage in the see me, feel me aspect of presidential campaigning, which typically requires a candidate's persistent physical presence and is particularly important in the earliest-voting states. So his only option is to campaign full bore once he leaves the governor's office in January, as though he's running without hesitation or qualification. Then, if Harris jumps into the contest, Newsom can sulk his way back to California, or break his pledge and run against her after saying he wouldn't. That, as Newsom suggested to Tapper, would be a gift to the rest of the Democratic field. Not too long ago, Newsom and Harris were carping over whether he was sufficiently supportive of her hurried-up 2024 presidential bid. In her account of the campaign, Harris said she reached out to the governor shortly after President Biden announced he was standing aside in favor of his vice president. When she called, Harris wrote, Newsom texted that he was out hiking and would call her back. But, she said, he never did. Much backing and forthing ensued — Newsom pointing out he didn't hesitate to endorse Harris once he returned to civilization — with both insisting all the while things are fine between them, really. Now the two are once more entwined, their fates tied up in mutual ambition and a shared hunger for the White House. Was Newsom's CNN interview a feint? Was he just faking respect for Harris as a way to keep in the good graces of Black women voters, all the while hoping against hope she won't run — and planning to reverse himself if she does? Will Harris put off her decision, knowing that every day and month that passes deepens the suspense and leaves Newsom twisting? Will the two finally collide head-on, settling once and for all their intense, if unspoken, competition? So much drama! Stay tuned. There’s a reality TV show in there somewhere. news.title: How the battle for Pelosi's seat ignited a bitter San Francisco Democratic showdown
news.text: After being securely held for nearly four decades by one of the most preeminent politicians in California history, the House seat to represent bright blue San Francisco in Congress is up for grabs in November — and dividing the Democratic Party. Rep. Nancy Pelosi (D-San Francisco), 86, the powerful former House Speaker who's held the seat since 1987, announced last year that she would not run again. In May, she passed over state Sen. Scott Wiener (D-San Francisco) — a prolific California legislator long considered a potential successor — to endorse San Francisco Supervisor Connie Chan, a local progressive with less legislative experience but strong support from labor. Pelosi's endorsement sent Chan, who had been languishing in polls, surging past Democratic tech millionaire Saikat Chakrabarti in the June primary. Chan finished with nearly 30% of the vote and Chakrabarti took 18%. Wiener won, with nearly 41% of the vote. Both Wiener, a gay man and staunch advocate for the city's large LGBTQ+ community, and Chan, who immigrated to the city from Hong Kong at age 13 and has deep ties to its large Chinese and immigrant communities, would make history by winning. Wiener would be the first out LGBTQ+ person to represent the city in Congress, and Chan the first Asian American immigrant woman. The race has sharply divided the state's Democratic establishment as a rare intraparty showdown between a deft legislator who has driven liberal California policy for years and a rising progressive with the powerful imprimatur of the icon they seek to replace. Both acknowledge they would take the same or similar positions on many issues, and fiercely oppose President Trump's agenda. But they also say San Franciscans face a real choice between them that will help define the city for years. "There is a clear cut between the two of us," Chan said. "He has long enjoyed establishment support and industry support, and we've been grassroots, on the ground, [Asian American and Pacific Islander] community, working people and labor unions — in collaboration and coalition building." "We need Democrats who are willing to fight — to fight in a smart way, and to fight in an aggressive way, to defeat Donald Trump and to lower the cost of living," Wiener said. "We are past the time where we need Democrats in office who were just going along to get along, or who, like Connie Chan, are just part of the status quo." Wiener, 56, has lived in the Castro neighborhood since 1997 and was a deputy city attorney and local Democratic Party chair before being elected to the Board of Supervisors in 2010. He was elected in 2016 to the state Senate, where he's had a massive influence, authoring more than 100 bills that have been signed into law. Allies and critics say he is a workhorse, and at times both effective and divisive. Wiener has been endorsed by the state and local Democratic parties; a slew of state leaders including California Atty. Gen. Rob Bonta, state Senate President Pro Tempore Monique Limón (D-Santa Barbara) and Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas (D-Hollister); various queer and labor groups including AFSCME; more than half the city's supervisors; and various members of Congress. Wiener has passed some of the state's most progressive laws on LGBTQ+ rights, including protections for gender-affirming care, and challenged federal immigration agents in California. He has also pushed progressive laws — backing safe injection sites, extending bar hours until 4 a.m., decriminalizing psychedelic drugs — that have put some of his fellow Democrats in uncomfortable spots when forced to vote on the controversial issues. Some in San Francisco label him a moderate, though that designation would draw laughs elsewhere in the country and even in Sacramento. Wiener is one of the most reviled state politicians on the conservative right nationally, and has received scores of death threats for his work, particularly on transgender issues. His website touts a laundry list of profane and homophobic attacks from MAGA loyalists — Elon Musk called him a "scumbag," former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene called him a "communist groomer" — that he wears as a badge of honor. On housing, Wiener has pushed for deregulation and development near transit hubs statewide to solve the housing and affordability crises, riling some homeowners averse to increased density and some progressives who say his plan favors developers and threatens existing rent-controlled housing. On tech, Wiener has pushed for artificial intelligence regulation but also been criticized for taking a technocratic approach with buy-in from wealthy tech leaders. Wiener has passed laws protecting net neutrality, capping prescription costs and mandating mental health parity, ending mandatory minimum sentences for nonviolent drug offenders, and requiring corporations disclose their greenhouse gas emissions. He has received substantial financial support from tech leaders and opposes Proposition 40, the ballot measure that seeks to impose a one-time tax on the state's billionaires. Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Long Beach), also gay and a former Long Beach mayor, said he considers Wiener a friend but also a generational legislator who has "led the country" on LGBTQ+ rights and housing policy. "I don't think there's a better legislator in the United States on housing," Garcia said. Rep. Laura Friedman (D-Glendale), who worked with Wiener for years in the state Legislature, said he has been a champion for many issues important to Californians — including the environment — while holding big industry accountable and backing labor. She said while many politicians decide to either rack up easy wins with legislation that barely moves the needle or focus on "progressive value signaling" without accomplishing much of anything, Wiener "takes on some of the most difficult and controversial progressive issues and really gets them done." Nancy Tung, the local Democratic Party chair, said many San Francisco politicians "recede" from the city's raucous local policy debate once they reach higher office, but Wiener is "still is in the knife fight," especially on housing and affordability issues — showing he cares about the city and making him "such a good fit" for Congress. Tung said she understands the appeal of sending a fellow Asian American woman to Congress in this political moment, but that Chan "just does not have the legislative record that Scott has." Chan, 47, who lived in a rent-controlled Chinatown apartment after immigrating with her mother and younger brother, now lives with her firefighter husband and son in the Richmond neighborhood. She was a community and legislative aide for years — including for then-Dist. Atty. Kamala Harris — before being elected to the Board of Supervisors in 2020. She has served as budget chair since 2023 and has centered her campaign, largely funded by Pelosi's network, around what she calls her "career fighting for working people." Chan has been endorsed by a host of Congress members, including Pelosi and Sen. Adam Schiff (D-Calif.); major labor groups including the California Federation of Labor Unions and the California Teachers Assn.; various progressive organizations and fellow and former supervisors; former mayor and S.F. power broker Willie Brown; and Chakrabarti, who since the primary has shared his campaign staff and funding with her. Chan, who supports Proposition 40, has helped create a $400-million reserve fund in San Francisco to make up for federal cuts to Medicaid and housing subsidies. She also passed a supplemental budget to fund immigration defense services for people targeted by the Trump administration and passed various labor-friendly measures, including a minimum wage increase for in-home workers and cost-of-living adjustments for city service workers. Pelosi said Chan "understands that budgets are statements of our values," has "championed justice and progress for working families" and "brings an important lived experience to this moment" as an immigrant woman. Schiff said Chan has impressed him as "a very powerful voice for those who are disenfranchised" and someone with "the potential of growing into" a leader like Pelosi. Kim Tavaglione, executive director of the San Francisco Labor Council, said she encouraged Pelosi to endorse Chan because Chan "supports San Francisco values," listens to labor and is a great strategist. Cleve Jones, the San Francisco activist who has fought for gay political representation since Harvey Milk's historic 1977 election to the Board of Supervisors, said Wiener "has done some very good things, particularly around LGBTQ issues and HIV/AIDS," but also angered some in the LGBTQ+ community by repeatedly showing up to an annual Trans March that organizers ask politicians not to attend. Wiener, who is Jewish, was aggressively heckled at this year's march, namely for his stance on the Israeli war in Gaza, which he was slower than other progressives to label a genocide. Conservatives mocked him for being targeted by his base, and Wiener ended up fundraising off the incident — which Jones said was "so cynical." He said Wiener's "loyalty is to big developers, big tech and big real estate," and that he "doesn't really see the urgency of yet another white man elected to Congress" when San Francisco can send a stronger message by electing Chan, an immigrant woman of color. Chan said she is a "pragmatic" progressive who has balanced the city's budget while protecting "healthcare, education, immigration resources" and other working-class priorities. She said Wiener is focused on deregulation for market-rate housing development, whereas she has prioritized tenants' rights and protecting existing rent-controlled housing in her push for affordable units. Chan said she will "walk and chew gum at the same time" in Washington by working for affordability while battling Trump, including by reversing his healthcare cuts, expanding Medicaid, providing affordable childcare, abolishing U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement and finally figuring out meaningful immigration reform. "I'm not sugarcoating it as if it's easy. But we gotta be able to find ways to work together to push those things forward," she said. Wiener said he and Chan share the goal "of getting Trump and MAGA out of office, and then making sure that people never feel tempted to flirt with authoritarianism again." But he said the way to do that is to advance policies that will "lower people's cost of living and make people's lives more sustainable" — including by passing universal healthcare, building millions of new homes, creating low-cost child care and leading a clean energy transition — and that he is the only candidate in the race with a proven ability to do that. "This is a race to succeed the most effective and operational member of Congress in modern American history," Wiener said. "San Francisco should send someone who actually has a track record, a proven track record, of being able to deliver."
news.summary: The race to replace Rep. Nancy Pelosi (D-San Francisco) in Congress has divided the progressive city and state Democrats more broadly, splitting them between a prolific gay state legislator and a Chinese immigrant city supervisor with Pelosi's imprimatur.
news.author: Kevin Rector

news.title: Trump’s desperate gerrymandering scheme backfires in Texas and Florida as voters sour on GOP
news.text:
Former federal prosecutor and Army National Guard infantry captain Eric Flores was considered a top recruit for the Republican Party in this year’s midterm elections. A newly redrawn Texas congressional map appeared to give him a clear shot at unseating longtime Democratic Rep. Vicente Gonzalez in a district that backed Donald Trump during the last presidential election.

However, Flores is now entangled in a far tougher contest than expected. Republican-led state legislatures followed Trump's call to undertake an unusual redistricting push to preserve their majority in the U.S. House, but the strategy is facing headwinds.

The GOP aimed to gain as many as nine congressional seats across Texas and Florida. Yet despite redrawing boundary lines to favor their candidates, the party is struggling under voter dissatisfaction over the economy, tariffs, the president’s deportation agenda, and the conflict with Iran.

The high-stakes nature of these contests has prompted Vice President JD Vance to head to Texas on Wednesday to campaign alongside Flores, before heading to Florida on Thursday.

Meanwhile, Rep. Suzan DelBene, chair of the House Democrats’ national campaign arm, recently toured Florida congressional districts targeted by Republicans.

"Republicans arrogantly thought they were going to redistrict seats to pick up more," DelBene said in an interview during her trip. "Instead, what they have is people across the state souring on the Republican agenda."

In response, House Republicans’ campaign spokesman Mike Marinella insisted the GOP can still achieve success this cycle "with a more favorable map, historic fundraising and spending advantages, stronger candidates and a common-sense agenda."

When Donald Trump returned to power two years ago, Republicans secured 25 of Texas’ 38 seats in the U.S. House.

Central to that ambition was the Rio Grande Valley, a predominantly Latino area at the southern tip of Texas that has trended toward Trump in recent cycles.

Texas’ 34th Congressional District, where Flores is competing, encompasses portions of the valley and supported Trump over Democrat Kamala Harris by 10 percentage points. Even so, Flores anticipates a tight contest, pointing to his opponent’s five terms of incumbency.

Flores earned Trump’s endorsement—which remains pinned at the top of his X profile—and delivered a speech at Trump's midterm convention in Dallas. However, in an effort to appeal to broader general election voters, he quietly removed a pledge to "SUPPORT PRESIDENT TRUMP’S AGENDA" from his campaign website.

"If I tell them the red meat issues or I tell them, you know, oh, Republican, Democrat, or anything like that, you lose them," Flores told The Associated Press. "I just sell them myself, sell them what I stand for."

GOP strategists in Washington acknowledge that economic pressures, including inflation and Trump’s tariffs, alongside the military involvement in Iran, have complicated their electoral strategy. Additionally, frustration among Latino voters over the president’s deportation agenda has unsettled GOP projections.

The party also faces vulnerability regarding its own incumbents in reconfigured territories. Rep. Monica De La Cruz, seeking a third term, is locked in a competitive battle against musician Bobby Pulido. A Latin Grammy winner whose most popular track has racked up 619 million streams on Spotify, Pulido has a level of name recognition rarely enjoyed by first-time challengers.

"I want a picture!" 42-year-old Eloise Ibarra shouted as Pulido navigated the stands at a high school football game. Ibarra indicated she would "probably" cast her ballot for Pulido after opting not to participate in the previous presidential contest.

"I don’t really like his policies," she remarked regarding Trump. "It’s very expensive, I go to the grocery store and buy $50 worth of stuff and it’s like five items."

Democratic organizers contend that the GOP overplayed its hand in redrawing the lines.

"I think Republicans counted on Hispanics, and they counted on rural Texas, to deliver votes for them, and these are the two places that are hurting the most," said Terri Burke of the Texas Democratic Party. Addressing the redistricting effort, she added, "this is really no longer such a slam dunk for the Republicans anywhere."

In Florida, where Republicans currently hold 20 of 28 congressional seats, party leaders sought to increase their tally to 24 through redrawn boundaries. Similar to Texas, those boundary changes relied heavily on 2024 results, when voters—particularly within Latino communities—expressed discontent with Democratic President Joe Biden over economic conditions and border security.

The GOP map sought to squeeze Rep. Kathy Castor in the Tampa area and Rep. Darren Soto near Orlando, while forcing South Florida Democratic Reps. Jared Moskowitz and Debbie Wasserman Schultz into the same district.

Rather than face a primary against a colleague, Moskowitz relocated his candidacy to an adjacent, Republican-leaning district, while Wasserman Schultz opted to run in a separate, strongly Democratic seat. Though Castor and Soto face tougher paths in their newly configured territories, DelBene maintains that both candidates can win under current conditions.

The redrawn map did not deter Pia Dandiya, an Ivy League-educated school principal and daughter of Indian immigrants, from launching her initial bid for Congress.

Dandiya is contesting Florida’s 22nd Congressional District, a seat Trump carried by double digits in 2024 and where Republicans originally anticipated a primary clash between Moskowitz and Wasserman Schultz.

However, Dandiya points out that Biden won the same set of precincts against Trump in 2020. Describing herself as "a happy road warrior," she frequently logs more than 150 miles between campaign stops.

"The way this district has been drawn just shows yet again that we are living in a world where elected officials are choosing voters instead of voters choosing elected officials, and it should never be that way," Dandiya said. DelBene and the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee have designated her campaign a priority as part of their "Red to Blue" initiative.

Dandiya maintains that voters are focusing on current economic realities rather than past party lines.

"Cost of living is not an issue that is exclusively impacting Democrats. It is an issue that is ubiquitous," she noted, adding that these financial concerns resonate across the more conservative pockets of her district as well.
news.summary: Republicans hoped to pick up as many as nine seats between Texas and Florida
news.author: Jesse Bedayn

news.title: Harry Enten Spots Stunning Shift ‘Ripping The Heart Out Of’ Donald Trump’s Presidency
news.text:
CNN chief data analyst Harry Enten has highlighted two polling trends that could spell serious trouble for Donald Trump and the GOP ahead of the 2026 midterm elections.

White, non-college voters “were the heartbeat of President Trump’s three presidential campaigns and, right now, the heartland is ripping the heart out of Donald Trump’s presidency,” Enten said on Tuesday’s broadcast of “CNN This Morning.”

Enten noted that Trump enjoyed a 25-point advantage over Democratic rival Kamala Harris among the group ahead of the 2024 election, but is now “in the negative,” with a net approval rating of -2 points.

“He’s in the negative territory with a group of voters that fueled his three presidential bids and allowed him to win a second term in the White House back in 2024,” Enten said. “We’re talking a drop here with the key core group of Donald Trump’s presidential campaigns, of 27 points away from the president of the United States. No wonder he’s so low.”

Trump has “always been reliant” on the group and “now even they have turned on him,” he added.

Watch here:

Enten then turned to inflation, which he said was “the key reason why Donald Trump won a second term in the White House.”

Trump’s net approval rating on the issue among white, non-college voters has sunk from +24 points in 2024 to -39 points now.

“Oh my. Oh my goodness gracious,” Enten said. “That’s a change of 63 points in the wrong direction, on the key issue that got Donald Trump reelected to a second term, among the key group that got him reelected.”

news.title: Democrats eye Nebraska as an opportunity to take a Senate seat away from Republicans
news.text: OMAHA, Neb. — Marine Corps veteran Gunner Arellano is a Donald Trump man — he voted for the president three times — but, he said, he won’t be casting a ballot for Sen. Pete Ricketts, R-Neb., in November. Dan Osborn, an independent who has the backing of the state’s Democratic Party, is “more for the people” than Ricketts, Arellano, a 35-year-old tobacconist, said in an interview at the S.G. Roi cigar shop in downtown Omaha late last month. While Arellano is familiar with Ricketts, a former two-term governor who ranks high on the list of wealthiest senators, he said that the senator isn’t present enough. “All those politicians, they want to come around when it’s election time, right?” he said. “Come down on a Wednesday in the middle of your term, you know.” Arellano said he’ll vote for Osborn, and voters like him are the reason that Democrats in Nebraska and at the national level hope they might be able to swipe a Senate seat in this heavily Republican state. They’re even more optimistic about flipping the state’s Omaha-based 2nd Congressional District, where Democratic presidential nominee Kamala Harris won in 2024 and Republican Rep. Don Bacon is retiring. In that year, Osborn surprised many political observers by running a competitive campaign against Sen. Deb Fischer, R-Neb., who ended up winning by a little more than 6 percentage points while Trump took the state by 20 points. The latter margin is one reason, along with Ricketts’ record of winning statewide races at the gubernatorial and Senate levels, that Republicans are confident they can keep the seat. Omaha was the last in an eight-stop, five-state tour that NBC News reporters took through battleground congressional districts — and states with competitive Senate races — along Interstate 80 in late August. Democrats need a net gain of four Senate seats to take control of the chamber next year, and Nebraska has emerged at the edge of the small list of states that could be in play in November. While there hasn’t been much in the way of independent polling of the state, Republicans are facing into a national wind as Trump’s approval ratings have cratered. Amid the ongoing war with Iran, rising prices for gas and diesel fuel, and Trump tariff policies that have wreaked havoc on rural America, Democrats see a resurgence of a brand of prairie populism that they believe will boost their candidates here in the heartland. That’s why Democrats say they aren’t as worried as they might be about an influx of GOP ad spending on the race, both from Ricketts and outside groups. Since Sept. 1, the Republican side has spent $7 million on the air, with another $8 million booked before Election Day, according to AdImpact data analyzed by NBC News. Osborn and groups backing him have spent $3.5 million and have reserved another $1.5 million. The money differential suggests Republicans are concerned about holding a seat that has been in their hands since 1997 — or at least committed to making sure they don’t take victory for granted. “I think you’re going to see, when Pete starts defining him [Osborn], and some of the outside groups come in to do that, then it’s going to go back to a safe red seat for us,” David McIntosh, president of the Club for Growth, which is backing Ricketts, said in an interview in early September. Jane Kleeb, the chair of the Nebraska Democratic Party, said in a telephone interview that she believes the money won’t be dispositive because Republicans and Ricketts have worn out their welcome. “Basically, voters are saying, ‘We’re not buying what you’re selling,’” she said. “So it’s not going to matter.” Most Republicans will stick with Ricketts, but some see Osborn as a candidate they will — or could — vote for. “Working man, union guy, seems grounded in the ways of Nebraska, an outsider,” said Chris Holder, 45, of Elkhorn, who works as a business analyst at Union Pacific Railroad. “I haven’t really vetted Osborn a whole bunch, but I am giving him consideration.” It’s an easy sale for Democrats here. Sally Guest, 48, a registered nurse whose husband, Larry, no longer works after an accident, said the two of them, both Democrats, are eager to vote for Osborn. “Pete Ricketts is the millionaire class, and he’s not served Nebraska well,” Sally said. “So I hope we don’t get any more of Pete Ricketts.” The Guests are acutely aware of health insurance costs because of her job and his disability, Sally said. Ricketts voted for Trump-backed legislation that cut back on the Affordable Care Act and Medicaid. The Guests have insurance for him but not for her — she pays for medical care out of pocket — because of the price. “God forbid I have a medical emergency or end up in the emergency room for an accident,” she said. “I’ll have to — I don’t know — I’d be better off dying.” But Todd Going, a business development manager in Omaha, said he plans to vote for Ricketts. A onetime Democrat, the 57-year-old Going said that party’s leftward movement — across the country, not just in Nebraska — makes him wary of voting to give it more power. “There’s been a total flip-flop on what party is representing the working class and the taxpayers,” he said. “And now I see the Democrat Party as totally different than even when I switched. It’s even more so. You see the socialists and the communists thing going on — what’s happening in all these elections all over the country, it’s very concerning to me.” At the House level, all the Republicans who spoke to NBC News said they plan to vote for Brinker Harding, an Omaha city councilman who is trying to re-create the kind of electorate that voted for Bacon three times. National Republicans say it’s a tough race — one of two currently held by Republicans that the Cook Political Report rates as leaning toward Democrats — but they believe Harding is hitting his marks. “Brinker Harding is a business leader and public servant with a record of results in Nebraska who is building a coalition of Republicans, Democrats and independents alike who believe in his vision of common sense over crazy,” Zach Bannon, a spokesman for the National Republican Congressional Committee, said, adding that Harding is “poised to win this November.” His opponent, Democrat Denise Powell, won a crowded primary earlier this year. The Guests said they don’t know much about her, but they will, as Larry put it, “vote blue” in a district that Democrats call the “blue dot” because it sometimes goes for their party in presidential elections while the rest of the state and most neighboring states typically vote Republican red. While Harding is portraying Powell as too extreme for the district, she is tying him as tightly as she can to Trump. So are national Democrats. “Nebraska voters want someone who will go to Congress and fight for them, not another party rubber stamp,” said Madison Andrus, a spokeswoman for the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, adding that Harding “bends the knee to Donald Trump.”

news.title: ‘Woke’ is dead. ‘Weird’ is back.
news.text:
“Woke” is out — but “weird” is back in. 

In 2024, Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz helped Democrats land on a clear message: President Donald Trump and his allies were “weird.” Two years later, facing steep midterms odds, Republicans are giving Democrats a taste of their own medicine.

Some of the GOP’s standard-bearers keep trying to make “weird” great again.

Sen. Tim Scott, R-S.C., needed less than 10 minutes at the Republican convention in Dallas earlier this month to call Democrats “dangerous, radical and weird” three times, singling out Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed. Vice President JD Vance also called El-Sayed “evil” and “weird” after the Michigan Democrat mentioned Vance’s wife.

Even President Donald Trump has joined in, repeatedly calling Texas Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico “weird” for his past remarks on gender identity, Christianity and transgender children and for allegedly being a vegan (Talarico says he is not.) On Friday, the president’s super PAC, MAGA Inc., released a 30-second ad that opens by calling Talarico “weird — very weird.”

The GOP’s turn to the schoolyard taunt comes as Republicans face stiff headwinds in the midterms. Trump is historically unpopular, consumer confidence continues sliding as inflation persists, and gas is still above $4 a gallon, with the war against Iran raging more than seven months after it began.

“When you can't talk about your successful record on the economy, you do ridiculous things like calling people ‘weird,’” Mike Madrid, a longtime Republican strategist who co-founded the anti-Trump Lincoln Project, told MS NOW.

Madrid said the tactic “reeked of desperation” when Democrats used it in 2024, “and it's even more desperate now because it's not even original — it’s a photocopy of desperation.”

The term took off in July 2024, when Walz called Trump and his allies “weird” during an interview on MS NOW’s “Morning Joe” two weeks before then-Vice President Kamala Harris named him her running mate. Walz later told “60 Minutes” he was describing Republicans’ “behaviors,” including “being obsessed with people's personal lives in their bedrooms and their reproductive rights, [and] making up stories about folks legally here eating cats and dogs.” Walz’s office did not respond to a request for comment.

The “weird” label quickly became a cornerstone of Democrats’ otherwise muddled messaging in the frantic run-up to the 2024 election. It seemed to work as a rejoinder to Republicans’ insistence that Democrats’ stances on issues like abortion, transgender rights and education were outside the mainstream.

Part of its appeal was that it played on people’s innate desire to belong, and on the assumption they wouldn’t want to support a candidate considered “weird,” according to Madeline Jalbert, an assistant professor of psychology at Western Washington University who wrote about the Democrats’ use of the term in 2024.

“These more extreme, harmful ideas, when you call them ‘weird,’ it communicates that they don't have social consensus,” Jalbert said.

In a 2024 essay, Jalbert and a colleague called the tactic “weird-checking.” They argued that in a post-truth era, it could land in a way that fact-checking just doesn’t.

“This is a way to call out opinions and ideas that doesn't require that you actually dig at all into the facts behind things,” Jalbert told MS NOW.

But ultimately, “weird” wasn’t a winning message.

“Voters wanted to know in 2024, and want to know now, who will make their lives better or worse, and ‘weird’ does not really get to that,” said Geoff Garin, president of Hart Research, a polling firm that worked with the Harris campaign. He told MS NOW the “weird” attack did not poll well internally. (A Democratic National Committee spokesperson declined to share specific data.)

A Democratic operative told MS NOW that Republicans' reliance on “weird” suggests they are “in panic mode.”

Republicans, though, seem undeterred. 

Asked for comment about Republicans’ use of the term this cycle, Bernadette Breslin, national press secretary of the National Republican Senatorial Committee, was unapologetic. “A Democrat in Maine procreated with his cousin, Abdul El-Sayed equated transgender surgeries to circumcision, and Mary Peltola required staff to feed her pet chameleon,” she said. “Weird is an understatement, and unlike Democrats, our reasons are based on facts.” (The “Democrat in Maine” is a reference to Troy Jackson, whose longtime partner is his second cousin.)

Natalie Baldassarre, national press secretary for the Republican National Committee, dismissed a question about whether Republicans floated the term in focus groups before deploying it.

“No studying is needed to see that an unmarried 37-year-old man who's obsessed with trans kids or a very angry little man who makes cringey social media videos are both, in fact, weird,” she said, referring to Talarico and El-Sayed, respectively.

In response to a request for comment from MS NOW, Cole Wozniak, a spokesperson for the El-Sayed campaign, said the candidate was “not concerned about the sounds coming from Washington — he’s going to continue to crisscross Michigan talking to voters about his plans to get money out of politics, put money in your pocket, and pass Medicare for All.”

A spokesperson for the Talarico campaign did not respond to a request for comment from MS NOW by publication time. 

This is not the first time that Republicans have co-opted language previously used by Democrats. They famously turned “woke” from an earnest progressive watchword into a derisive shorthand for virtue-signaling.

But “weird” lacks the punch of “woke,” according to Drew Westen, a psychology professor and longtime political strategist. He said “woke” captured “a pervasive feeling among the public, across party lines,” about policing speech and identity. “Weird” doesn’t wield the same power — especially when it’s deployed against some of the Democrats’ most magnetic speakers, like Talarico and El-Sayed.

“They’re trying to turn charismatic candidates into ‘weirdness,’” said Westen, author of “The Political Brain: The Role of Emotion in Deciding the Fate of the Nation.” “I think Republicans are throwing spaghetti against the wall because they’re so disliked by the public.”

With voters seemingly more worried about their wallets than “weirdness,” Madrid said the strategy is likely to fall flat for Republicans, just as it failed for Democrats.

“If it's the difference between putting in somebody who's ‘weird’ and driving up the price of gas,” he said, “we're at the point now where the average old white Republican is going to say, ‘Give me the weird guy.’”
news.author: Steve Benen

news.title: The surprising frontrunner to lead the Trump resistance (again)
news.text:
Welcome to Power Players, The i Paper’s opinion series in which our writers and experts take an in-depth look at the key figures in American politics as the US reshapes itself and the world.

• The ‘swamp creature’ eclipsing JD Vance in the race to succeed Trump• Netanyahu’s to blame for his American nightmare – and it spells his doom• The Democrat who has finally worked out how to beat Trump

Kamala Harris sure looks like she’s running for US President. The polls (volatile as they are right now) have the former vice president and 2024 presidential nominee as the Democratic front-runner.

There she was in late September on the stump in a crucial 2028 primary state, Michigan, campaigning for a Senate hopeful in a must-win 2026 race. “I have not decided if I’m going to run again,” Harris declared in Detroit, adding: “I do sincerely believe [20]28 won’t matter until we get through [20]26. When you focus on the thing over there, you trip on the thing right here.”

The road to becoming the Democratic presidential nominee – again – is full of trip hazards for Harris. While she may be campaigning in Michigan, Georgia and Nevada this fall, she’s not universally welcome on the stump.

It’s now less than five weeks until the midterm elections, which will decide which party controls Congress. Democratic candidates from Alaska to Kansas have shied away from being seen with Harris, fearing voters in those Republican-leaning states will see the former vice president as too left wing.

And therein lies the problem with Harris’s putative 2028 candidacy. Where’s the evidence that she can win votes across the US? She’s already tried and failed to win the presidency once – why would 2028 be any different?

Harris’s supporters say she was campaigning with one arm tied behind her back in 2024. President Joe Biden’s decision to drop out of the race weeks after his abysmal debate performance gave her only 107 days to campaign for the White House.

Harris fans say she couldn’t distance herself from Biden on the campaign trail because she was the incumbent vice president and had to remain loyal to the administration’s agenda. Anything else would have been inauthentic. This time, so the theory goes, Harris can run as herself. But who is she, and what does she really believe? The answers remain unclear.

Harris’s appearance with Senate candidate Abdul el-Sayed in Detroit gave political analysts much to chew on. For many, it looked like an attempt to build bridges within the Democratic coalition. After a divisive primary in which Black voters seemed to favour Sayed’s opponent, there was Harris, the first Black woman ever to be a major party presidential nominee, trying to persuade her strongest constituency to swing behind a man who needs their votes.

Appearing with Sayed, who is an outspoken critic of Israel and has called the war in Gaza a genocide against the Palestinians, was important for Harris. Gaza and the Biden administration’s support for Israel was a divisive issue in the 2024 election and contributed to Harris’s loss in Michigan, which has a sizeable Arab-American population.

If Harris runs again, she will need to court those voters who feel she did nothing stop Benjamin Netanyahu’s bombing of Gaza when she was in office. And if she wishes to be a kingmaker whose endorsement is critical in the 2026 race, she has some explaining to do on Gaza.

The new Democratic primary calendar favours a third Harris run for the White House (remember she ran against Biden in 2020) – at least in theory. The order in which states vote shapes the primaries enormously. It’s no longer the predominantly white states of Iowa and New Hampshire at the front of the queue. South Carolina votes first in 2028 – historically, Black voters have made up a large part of the Democratic primary electorate in that state, and its choice of Biden in 2020 marked a turning point in that primary.

Even so, David Plouffe, Harris’s 2024 senior adviser, was honest about the hurdles she would face. “Her strongest day will be her first day in the campaign,” Plouffe told Pod Save America, predicting that her support would probably erode as the race developed. Plouffe also predicted that the kind of candidates who do well nationwide in 2026 – when voters are sour on the economy and looking for change – will influence the shape of the 2028 presidential primary.

An Axios report recently found that a number of ex-Harris aides believe she ultimately won’t run for the White House in 2028, arguing she is a rational actor who is simply trying to maintain her influence within the party. The report added that donors still sore about her 2024 loss may not wish to open their wallets again.

Then there’s the media environment of today, already so different to 2024. Candidates now must be able to do everything from lengthy podcasts to live local TV slots while creating their own daily content in which they appear in touch with voters’ concerns.

Look at James Talarico in Texas, and Sayed in Michigan. This new world may not be Harris’s forte. As a steely lawyer she was formidable in her debate appearance against Donald Trump, but despite attempts to schedule an interview, she never sat down with podcaster Joe Rogan for one of those chatty free-wheeling appearances that are now the currency of the political realm.

She came of age in an era in which public appearances were tightly scripted. For now, Harris is drawing attention as she appears to test the waters for a 2028 run – and she, more than anyone, is only too aware of the pitfalls that may lie ahead.

news.title: AOC, Donald Trump Jr. Make Gains in New 2028 Poll
news.text: Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Donald Trump Jr. gained ground among voters considering potential 2028 presidential contenders in a new Harvard CAPS/Harris poll, while the leaders of the hypothetical Democratic and Republican fields saw their support slip. The shifts offer an early look at a 2028 race that is still taking shape, with none of the potential contenders tested in the poll having formally announced a campaign. Among Democrats, former Vice President Kamala Harris remains the leading choice at 38 percent, down 4 percentage points from August. California Governor Gavin Newsom followed at 17 percent, while Ocasio-Cortez climbed 3 points to 12 percent. Ocasio-Cortez has not yet decided whether she will run for president in 2028, saying she plans to weigh the decision after the midterm elections. In an interview with The New York Times published last week, Ocasio-Cortez discussed the challenges of a potential presidential campaign. “This country has never elected a female president. Why are we pretending that this is not a factor?” Ocasio-Cortez told the Times. “That doesn’t make it impossible, but to act as though it’s not a factor in anything ever is really a form of, like, denialism.” On the Republican side, Vice President JD Vance remained in first place at 39 percent in the poll, down 3 points from August. Trump Jr. jumped 6 points to 24 percent, followed by Marco Rubio at 17 percent. Trump Jr. has previously left open the possibility of a presidential run, but has also said he is not currently interested in running in 2028. ”I've always said, while I'll never 100% rule it out down the line, I have ZERO interest in running for office in 28 or anytime soon,” Trump Jr. wrote on X in May 2025. The Harvard CAPS/Harris poll was conducted online from September 26 to 28, 2026, among 2,200 registered voters. The survey has a margin of error of approximately plus or minus 2.1 percentage points. Newsweek reached out to representatives for both Ocasio-Cortez and Trump Jr. via email late Tuesday. What Voters Are Saying Ahead of Midterms More immediately, with just 35 days until the November election, the poll also found that 42 percent of voters have not firmly settled on their midterm choice. Twenty-six percent of those surveyed said they are leaning toward certain candidates but could still change their minds, while another 16 percent said they have not yet decided. Fifty percent said they have definitely made up their minds, according to the survey. On the economy, voters were closely divided when asked whether the economy is better or worse than it was when Joe Biden was president. Fifty-three percent said the economy today is worse, compared with 47 percent who said it is better. Among independent voters, 61 percent said the economy is worse today than it was under Biden, while 39 percent said it is better. The economy and inflation continue to top voters' concerns, with 45 percent saying inflation is the issue most important to them personally. Artificial intelligence also emerged as a notable issue, with 15 percent citing it as a top concern. Trump has continued to defend his economic record in recent days, saying the country has the “best economy we've ever had.” “We have the best employment numbers that came out in the history of our country. More people working today than at any time ever before,” Trump told reporters while departing the White House Sunday. He also reiterated that gas prices will fall once the Iran war ends, which he said will happen “soon.” The Trump administration is also considering a ban on U.S. diesel exports. Nationwide, drivers are paying an average $4.46 for a regular gallon of gas, and $6.44 for diesel, according to AAA. “With oil holding below $100 per barrel, many Americans may see modest declines ahead for gasoline and slight drops for diesel, but the West Coast faces continued pressure with further increases possible,” Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, said in a statement. “The broader geopolitical situation remains fluid and could push prices in either direction with little warning, and with Trump still weighing a diesel export ban, impacts could follow.” Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Edward T. Cummins
news.summary: New polling finds Harris and Vance leading their parties while AOC and Trump Jr. make gains.

news.title: Party insiders on how the Democrats defeat Trump: ‘Sewage socialism’, trust and $$$
news.text:
When voters go to the polls in the United States in November, they will face a midterm election that Donald Trump has made a referendum about himself. 

At the Republicans’ unusual midterm convention earlier this month, Trump asked voters to “vote as though [his] name is on the ballot.” His Vice President JD Vance asked voters for “another chance” while speaking on a podcast.

This tactic should produce an opening for the Democratic Party to define a different vision for the country. Recent polls give Democrats a massive advantage heading into this year’s midterms, but mostly as a vote against Trump’s Republican Party. The Democratic Party’s brand struggles with approval ratings near Trump’s own historic lows. 

The past decade has seen an internal struggle over what the party should be or become. It has lacked a clear identity and has never had a consistent strategy for opposing Trump, nor has it had success in articulating a clear vision beyond him. 

With the 2026 midterms coming to a close and the 2028 presidential primary just around the corner, I spoke with former colleagues who represent the future of the Democratic Party, from across factions and regions, about winning in 2026, the possibility of governing in 2027, and the path forward to 2028. 

How to win when partisanship is dead

The first question of the 2026 primary revolves around how candidates should treat Trump. Should they nationalise the race or keep issues local? 

Money certainly plays a role in the decision. When a race begins to receive national attention, donations flow in, but they also lose any independence they might have from their party’s brand. 

Lavanna Martinez, an independent consultant based in New Jersey who primarily works with national organisations outside the party’s formal infrastructure, told Crikey: “I think any campaign would be a fool to be focusing on anything other than the economy right now. Americans are feeling the financial squeeze in every part of their lives. We rarely get an opportunity to have every voter be a single-issue voter, and this is the year.”

Trump’s tariff regime and war in Iran are undeniably his, and cost of living remains the number one issue for American voters. Rodericka Applewhaite, communications director for Majority Democrats, told Crikey this will be a problem for the president: “Perhaps [Trump and economic messaging] would be more mutually exclusive if he hadn’t spent the last two years calling America’s affordability crisis a hoax, but for this particular cycle, they are one in the same.”

As Democrats negotiate this path, they have to contend with a political environment in which partisan loyalty has all but died. While 84% of voters who identify as Democrats view their party favourably, only 52% of Democratic-leaning independents do the same, according to a Pew poll. 

Corrina Jaramillo Feldman, a strategist who has held senior positions with many of New Mexico’s Democratic stars, including Secretary Deb Haaland and Rep. Melanie Stansbury, said that voters are moving away from identifying with the party and instead showing “loyalty to issues”. 

Jon Lovett, co-host of Pod Save America and former Obama speechwriter, recently told The New Yorker: “Across the board, I don’t know what this establishment of the Democratic Party stands for, and neither does this country.”

So while Democrats have spent a decade writing out policy positions, the public has had a difficult time making clear sense of what any of it means. 

Fox News polls going back to 2018 show clear majorities of the country don’t think that Democrats have a clear plan for the country, a problem that has only gotten worse over time. 

Lovett made the point that the party’s most progressive figures, like Senator Bernie Sanders and Mayor Zohran Mamdani, could sit down with conservative media figures and not lose trust with their voters, because their political positions were well established. But when an “establishment” Democrat does the same, it leaves voters feeling like they’ve been sold out. 

The main challenge Democratic candidates face is not in updating their policy agenda — which is broadly supported by the American population — but giving voters a reason to believe that those beliefs are held with more than an attachment to a fundraising check. 

That sureness allows those candidates to speak to a wider audience, and to go on conservative media without alienating their base voters. 

Is the key ‘sewage socialism’?

Democrats are ahead substantially in the race for the House, according to recent high-quality polls from Emerson College, Ipsos, and The Economist/YouGov. The RealClear Polling average has Democrats ahead by about 8.4 percentage points. 

State-level seats are harder to see from public polling, but four Republican-held governorships are rated as “toss-ups” by the nonpartisan Cook Political Report. Democrats would have to pick up a total of 19 state legislative seats to take control of state legislatures in Arizona, Michigan, Minnesota, and Wisconsin. 

Congressional Democrats have already begun to make plans for power. 

Democratic House Leader Hakeem Jeffries has set up working groups to draft an affordability agenda, and Democratic leader in the Senate Chuck Schumer said: “Lower costs are going to be the North Star now and through all of 2026”. 

Ricardo Gutierrez, a key organiser in the progressive movement with close ties to figures like Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Bernie Sanders, lays out a vision for what he calls “sewage socialism”. He told Crikey that the Democratic brand could be revived at the state and local level by “making sure that services are provided, covering potholes, making sure that the lights are on and schools are getting their services. That’s how we show up. Not something ethereal, not just pandering — actual very, very meaningful, tangible results.”

But at the national level, Democrats would not have unilateral power, even if they came in with majorities in both the House and the Senate. Trump — and Natalie Harp — wield a veto pen, and an evenly divided Senate gives its tie-breaking vote to Vice President JD Vance. 

“Voters would rather hear that we tried to make their lives more affordable and were blocked by this White House or state legislatures than deal with more excuses from the elected officials they put their trust in,” Applewhaite said.

The point, as Rep. Ro Khanna told The New Yorker, is to argue to the American people, “give us the White House [in 2028] so we can actually make this law.”

Congressional Democrats have weighed this exact question. Jamie Raskin and Robert Garcia have been named as key figures in the House’s oversight agenda, with leaders refusing to rule in or out the prospect of impeaching Trump or any members of his administration. 

“I absolutely do not think it should be a strategic priority for Democrats to block all of Trump’s appointees,” Martinez said, adding that the party should only be particularly aggressive on lifetime judicial appointments. 

She proposes that the Senate, under Democratic leadership, should “put together a public list of requirements for any appointee, and they should be generic gold standards that most Americans expect out of our government officials”.

Applewhaite calls this “pragmatism, rather than kneejerk partisanship”, which is what Americans “would like to see”.

Picking a new leader

To Gutierrez, the question then becomes who Democrats choose to lead the party in a majority. A new leader would be able to look toward the future, rather than rehashing the arguments of years past. 

But Washington is not the end of American domestic power. With more than 40,000 elected offices on the ballot this November — and an emphasis on delivering solid results in places where executive action is possible — Jaramillo Feldman pointed to what Democratic governors could do, citing environmental policies, land use, engaging with tribal communities, and rent stabilisation. 

Applewhaite, one of the most sought-after Democratic communications specialists, says that highlighting victories ought to be a priority that receives investment. She points to the administration of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, where “playground restorations get press conferences. Sophisticated social media strategies have been deployed for filling potholes.” Each of these tells voters that Democrats are working on their behalf. 

Mamdani in particular has become a benchmark for the Democratic movement, though he is constitutionally blocked from running for president because he was born in Uganda (and part of the same diaspora of Ugandan-born Indians that produced Charli XCX, whose mother was born in Uganda and fled to the UK as a child). 

As Democrats build their 2027 agenda, the 2028 presidential primary will rage on. Campaigns are expected to launch as early as December 2026, a full 14 months before the first votes are cast in South Carolina. 

Virtually no-one is willing to name a preferred candidate at this stage, with the field yet to develop. “There are a lot of smart, talented people being discussed,” Martinez said. “But I’m not ready to attach myself to any one candidate before we know what they are actually offering.”

Over this past weekend, I conducted a very informal poll of my Instagram followers. Not a representative sample of the Democratic electorate, but a good mix of the operatives who will lead campaigns in 2028 and beyond. 

I placed 21 candidates who have either expressed interest or been publicly discussed as candidates into brackets based on their last name. A clear top tier emerged from the first round: Stephen Colbert, Gavin Newsom, Gretchen Whitmer, Andy Beshear, Kamala Harris, Mark Kelly, Jon Ossoff, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Pete Buttigieg, and JB Pritzker. 

However, as the rounds went on, support consolidated around Buttigieg, Ossoff, and Ocasio-Cortez — each a young, charismatic figure with a strong social media presence. They span the ideological divide of the party, but each has a clear position. In the final round, Buttigieg narrowly won, though I got at least five unprompted comments that the American electorate wouldn’t be ready for an openly gay president, even if they personally supported him. 

The poll revealed six axes on which the primary debate will be shaped: economic ambition, institutional change, civil rights, corporate power, technological change, and political identity. 

On the major policies that will affect the 2028 primary, Gutierrez said that “corporate PACs and their influence and the presence of AI” will play a major role. Applewhaite agreed, saying that “AI will be huge, and the first candidate to offer a comprehensive (dare I say nuanced) answer for how it should be handled will earn serious attention.”

While Martinez said that the focus on economic affordability will continue: “I want to see who can offer a serious vision for making life more affordable.”

But who gets to make these arguments in 2028 and beyond is a different question. 

Martinez ran National Run for Office Day in 2021 as part of her role with Run for Something, the primary group recruiting and supporting young candidates for downballot office. “I have seen firsthand that there is no shortage of people who are interested in serving,” she said, but “the bigger problem is access and viability”. 

Running for office takes time and money, and establishing donor networks necessary for success can be a barrier that excludes potential candidates early. 

The new primary calendar will reshape the Democratic Party. For nearly 40 years, Iowa’s first-in-the-nation status meant that candidates who could appeal to Iowa’s largely rural, white, agricultural community had an advantage in the party apparatus. 

Now, the calendar prioritises more diverse states, with the first six, in order: South Carolina, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Mexico, Michigan, and Virginia. 

Applewhaite remarked that the old calendar had an effect on the party as a whole, “Presidential hopefuls could … appeal to white voters only and it showed, from the policies they prioritised to their personnel picks.”

A calendar that forces candidates to heavily engage with the demographically varied parts of the Democratic coalition will see a very different Democratic Party in the future. Candidates and operatives emerge from the limelight of the presidential nominating process with newfound money and attention — and prestige in a White House hiring process that has historically favoured early primary states as a kind of currency in return for early endorsements. 

The specifics of policy seem to matter less than just finding a generation of candidates who sound like they are saying what they believe.
news.summary:
After a crushing loss in 2024, the Democrats are still lost in the wilderness. Here's what insiders think is the party's path back to the White House, and how it can win in 2026.

news.title: Chris Cuomo Claims Ex-Prez Joe Biden Privately Admitted He 'Sabotaged' Democrats During 2024 Election: 'He Wanted to Punish Them'
news.text:
Chris Cuomo has claimed former President Joe Biden privately admitted that he "sabotaged" Democrats during the 2024 presidential election after party leaders pushed him to end his reelection campaign, RadarOnline has learned.

The NewsNation host made the claim during the September 24 episode of his podcast, The Chris Cuomo Project, arguing Biden was angry over the effort to replace him on the Democratic ticket and deliberately made the transition more difficult.'I Believe He Screwed Up the Process'Cuomo said people who have heard Biden speak privately told him the former president still acknowledges what he did.

"He was so p--sed that they didn't want him to run again, that I believe he submarined the whole thing,” Cuomo claimed. "I believe he forced (Kamala) Harris on them, I believe he delayed it, I believe he screwed up the process, I believe he wanted to punish them for not letting him run again. I really believe that."

Cuomo’s comments center on the chaotic period after Biden’s June 2024 debate against then-Republican presidential nominee Donald Trump.

Biden faced mounting pressure from Democratic lawmakers following the debate and announced July 21, 2024, that he would end his reelection bid. 

He endorsed then-Vice President Kamala Harris shortly afterward.Kamala Harris and Joe Biden’s Complicated Political RelationshipCuomo argued that Biden’s anger over being pushed aside influenced what happened next.

The journalist claimed Biden remained "very angry" about how Democrats handled the 2024 race and was so "disgusted" that he chose not to vote for Harris.

Cuomo did not provide details explaining how Biden allegedly "forced" Democrats to nominate Harris. He also did not identify the people he said had heard Biden acknowledge the alleged sabotage during private conversations.

Harris’ relationship with Biden became more complicated after the 2024 campaign.

When she inherited the Democratic nomination following his decision to end his reelection bid, during their four years in the White House, Harris publicly defended Biden.Kamala Harris Sounds OffIn a 2024 CNN interview, Harris recalled that Biden personally called her to tell her he had decided to withdraw from the race. "My first thought was not about me, to be honest with you. My first thought was about him," she said.

Her public tone changed after the election. In her memoir, Harris wrote that leaving the decision over Biden's reelection campaign to the former president and first lady Jill Biden was "recklessness," arguing that the stakes were too high for the decision to be treated as a personal matter.

By August 2026, Harris was also openly contrasting her approach with Biden’s earlier belief that Republicans could experience an “epiphany” after Trump left politics, saying Democrats cannot "sit around hoping Republicans will have an 'epiphany' and do the right thing."

Cuomo based his claim about Biden's alleged private admission on conversations with unnamed people who he said had heard the former president discuss the 2024 election.'He Will Still Tell People That He Did It'"He will still tell people that he did it," Cuomo said.

The allegation adds another explanation for one of the most consequential moments of the 2024 presidential campaign, when Biden ended his reelection bid and Harris quickly became the Democratic nominee.

Biden ultimately remained out of the race while Trump defeated Harris in the November election.

Cuomo's account, however, remains an allegation about Biden's private thinking and actions rather than an independently established explanation for the Democrats’ 2024 defeat.
news.summary: Chris Cuomo claims Joe Biden privately admitted to sabotaging Democrats in 2024 after party leaders pushed him out of the presidential race.

news.title: It’s Time to Start Ignoring the Polls
news.text:
My colleague Matt Margolis exposed a great example of this in Abdul El-Sayed Senate campaign in Michigan. Matt laid out in detail how El-Sayed has been ramming the message home about “Medicare for All,” which must be falling flat, because as Matt noted, “Now El-Sayed is suddenly all for people staying on private insurance if they want to. ‘If you would like to have a private insurer, above that, you're welcome to do that,’ El-Sayed says now, channeling his inner Barack Obama.”

What this dramatic pivot illustrates is that either the El-Sayed campaign is not faring as well as advertised by the left and the legacy media (and their polls), or the “Medicare for All” issue has become a liability for the candidate.

Abdul El-Sayed is a liar.El-Sayed has already called to completely eliminate private insurance at least 10 times. https://t.co/66BzAxjAXO pic.twitter.com/zuEC0B7C83— RNC Research (@RNCResearch) September 26, 2026

Clearly, the internals are telling the campaign something that the public polls are not saying. 

So, what are “public polls"? Those are the ones everyone in the news media is talking about incessantly right now. Leftist universities, NGOs, media organizations, activist groups, and others pay for them. They serve a very specific purpose, one every conservative should already know.

Public polls are designed to shape public opinion, not reflect it. They are designed to discourage conservative and Republican voters and embolden Democrat and leftist voters. They want to disenfranchise you. They want you to give up and decide not to vote, because they want you to feel that voting this time around is pointless. They want to suppress the vote for Republican candidates.

If a legacy media organization, including Fox News, attaches its name to a public poll, ignore it, especially right now. Between now and the final week before the election, pollsters will oversample Democrat voters and leftists to tilt the scales in favor of Democrat candidates. They will structure the questions to favor the Democrats. They will talk mostly to Democrats. They will shut out Republican candidates and ignore Republican and independent voters.

The Wall Street Journal provides us with a perfect example of how public polls are used to discourage you into giving up.

President Trump’s approval rating drops to 37% in a WSJ poll, the lowest of any president heading into a midterm election in Journal polls dating to 1990. 🔗 https://t.co/4CGJ8WscDh pic.twitter.com/haG1MGKPoM— The Wall Street Journal (@WSJ) September 28, 2026

Back in 2024, Matt Margolis wrote about another now-infamous “suppression poll” in Iowa that had Kamala Harris trouncing Trump in the state. Right before Election Day, Matt blew the lid off of those sketchy Iowa poll results coming out of Iowa when he wrote:

I warned you about suppression polls, and the mother of all suppression polls appears to have just dropped.And it's not even from a swing state.The latest Des Moines Register/Mediacom poll just dropped, and it claims that Kamala Harris has a three-point lead in Iowa.‘Kamala Harris now leads Donald Trump in Iowa — a startling reversal for Democrats and Republicans who have all but written off the state’s presidential contest as a certain Trump victory," the Des Moines Register reports. "A new Des Moines Register/Mediacom Iowa Poll shows Vice President Harris leading former President Trump 47% to 44% among likely voters just days before a high-stakes election that appears deadlocked in key battleground states.’

The Des Moines Register relied on veteran pollster J. Ann Selzer for a very long time up, until that poll. The poll Matt covered was her last one. She stopped doing election polling after this because President Donald Trump ended up winning the state by 13 points. The newspaper’s disgraceful “suppression survey” backfired on the left in a very red state.

One of the things the Des Moines Register did not do in 2024, but most legacy media organizations do during an election cycle, is shore up their results in the final days prior to the election. If you notice, the polls tend to tighten up right before the election. That’s mostly because pollsters can't afford to be wrong like Selzer was. They know they have to make sure their final polls before Election Day are more accurate so that no one can accuse them of being wrong or biased once the votes are counted.

But before that, pollsters will give themselves plenty of grace to weaponize their polls to suppress voter turnout among conservatives and boost voter turnout for Democrats.

Now that we’re just about to head into October, this would be a very good time to ignore those polls. Don't forget that only one poll counts: the one where you fill out a ballot and turn it in.

news.title: MS NOW star Molly Jong-Fast jokingly DEFENDS Trump after President, 80, appeared to nod off moments after attacking 'Sleepy Joe' Biden
news.text:
MS NOW commentator Molly Jong-Fast offered a sarcastic defense of Donald Trump after the President was roundly accused of falling asleep during a White House event on Monday.

The 2pm event was held to announce plans to bring a $15 billion steel mill to Iowa. 

Jong-Fast, 48, reacted to one of many clips showing Trump, 80, with his eyes closed at the event.

Riffing off the fact that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick had been stressing the importance of domestic steel production in the clip, Jong-Fast quipped on X: 'In trumps defense howard is very very boring.'

The 14 seconds of footage, shared by Kamala Harris's rebooted 2024 campaign X account, came from a longer White House feed where Trump is seen repeatedly reopening his eyes and speaking to attendees.

Politicians and commentators were still quick to accuse the conservative of falling asleep.

Trump also once again revived his sleep-related nickname for his predecessor, Joe Biden, during the Oval Office meeting, leading to a jab from his son, Hunter. 

'Sleepy who?' he wrote over an unflattering still of the President.

California Governor Gavin Newsom also got his licks in, via a post from his press office.

'President McConnell is looking great,' the office wrote on X, an off-color reference to 84-year-old Senator Mitch McConnell's recent health struggles. 

'I have no doubt in my mind that Donald Trump fell asleep multiple times today. He’s just tired, just like we’re all tired of him,' liberal commentator Brian Krassenstein wrote.

Aaron Rupar wrote: 'Trump is struggling to stay awake on camera.' 

The barb from Jong-Fast was only the latest from the cable news star this month to cast doubt on Trump's mental faculties, after Biden ended up abandoning his 2024 reelection run just months before the election.

'So sleepy,' the daughter of feminist author Erica Jong wrote in a Threads post published on September 18, in reaction to a post from the account 'DemsMight' with footage of a tired-looking Trump with his eyes closed at an event earlier in the day. 

A caption panned the conservative as 'an embarrassment.' 

After critics accused Trump of falling asleep at a Washington, DC, 9/11 ceremony, Jong-Fast wrote on X: 'It’s weird that the president keeps falling asleep in the middle of the day, but it’s even weirder that this isn’t more of a scandal.

'But what do I know I’ve been worrying about climate change this whole time when I should have been worried about an AI apocalypse,' the post continued.

When Rupar shared a clip of Trump with his eyes closed during an event in the Oval Office with travel industry executives the day before back on September 2, Jong-Fast took to Threads to proclaim: 'Is anyone worried that the president can’t stay awake?'

White House spokesperson Davis Ingle proclaimed: 'Anyone claiming the President was asleep is lying,' when approached for comment Tuesday by the Daily Mail

'President Trump’s sharpness, unmatched energy, and historic accessibility stand in stark contrast to what we saw during the last administration when Democrats and the legacy media intentionally covered up Joe Biden’s serious mental and physical decline from the American people,' Ingle said in a statement.

'President Trump is the sharpest and most accessible President in American history who is working nonstop to solve problems and deliver on his promises, and he remains in excellent health.'

Jong-Fast runs a political podcast, Fast Politics with Molly Jong-Fast, in addition to her MS NOW duties.

Her expertise lies in Washington, but she wrote an op-ed for The New York Times last month surrounding the stigma female patients face when undergoing plastic surgeries. 

She detailed her recent decision to get a face- and neck-lift in the piece. 

'My face, for instance, is directly connected to my livelihood,' she wrote at a point, noting that she discusses 'politics on TV for a living.'

'What I did to my face isn’t that unusual; I’d argue that it’s actually the norm for women on TV these days.'

She released a memoir surrounding her upbringing under her 84-year-old mother early last year. The book painted the pair's relationship as 'complicated' and one that 'can really mess you up.
news.summary: The 2pm event where Trump was filmed with his eyes closed for a prolonged period surrounded plans to bring a $15 billion steel mill to Iowa.
news.author: Alex Hammer,Editor

news.title: We Asked Trump's New AI Government Site About His Controversial Claims
news.text: The Trump administration's newly launched America.gov chatbot provided direct answers Tuesday to a series of questions about the 2020 election, presidential term limits, impeachment proceedings and other politically sensitive topics when Newsweek tested the system shortly after its debut. The administration has promoted the AI-powered platform as a tool that draws information from official government sources and could become a public-facing gateway to federal information. The answers could also intensify scrutiny over how government AI systems handle politically sensitive subjects as federal agencies increasingly deploy artificial intelligence tools. Newsweek submitted 15 prompts to the chatbot between 12:54 p.m. and 1:06 p.m. ET, asking about election results, alleged election fraud, climate science, presidential salaries, impeachment history, criminal convictions and Trump's eligibility to seek a third term. In each case reviewed by Newsweek, the chatbot cited government records, constitutional provisions, federal agencies or other official sources as the basis for its answer. Newsweek has reached out to the White House for comment. Trump's New AI Government Website: What to Know America.gov is designed to pull information from federal agencies and present it through a chatbot-style interface. Rather than searching separate government websites, users can enter questions or requests and receive answers sourced from official government information. Officials compared the experience to consumer AI platforms, saying that the system is intended to guide users through government processes and explain requirements for services such as Medicare enrollment, disaster assistance and federal job applications. The current version is primarily focused on providing information and helping users find answers. It can explain procedures and direct users to relevant resources, but it cannot yet complete many government transactions on a user's behalf. Who Won the 2020 Presidential Election? At 12:54 p.m. ET, Newsweek asked the chatbot: "Who won the 2020 presidential election?" The system answered, "Joseph R. Biden Jr. won the 2020 U.S. presidential election," citing Electoral College results showing Biden received 306 electoral votes to Donald Trump's 232. It also linked to National Archives records and Federal Election Commission results. The chatbot delivered the same conclusion when Newsweek returned to the topic later in the testing period. Asked again twice at 1:01 p.m. "Who lost the 2020 presidential election?" and "Did Donald Trump lose the 2020 election?" it again answered that Biden won and cited the same records. Was There Widespread Fraud That Changed the Result of the 2020 Election? At 12:55 p.m. ET, Newsweek asked: "Was there widespread fraud that changed the result of the 2020 election?" The chatbot responded: "Official U.S. government sources did not find widespread fraud that changed the 2020 presidential election result." It cited findings from federal agencies, election officials and intelligence reviews and stated that while isolated irregularities can occur, official reviews and recounts did not identify fraud on a scale that altered the outcome. Can Donald Trump Run for President in 2028? At 12:56 p.m. ET, Newsweek asked: "Can Donald Trump run for president in 2028?" The chatbot answered: "No. Under the 22nd Amendment, no person may be elected President more than twice. Donald Trump has already been elected President twice (2016 and 2024), so he cannot be elected again in 2028." It added that another election victory would require a constitutional amendment changing the existing term-limit provision and cited the text of the Constitution's 22nd Amendment.
